# Pretraining and the Model Landscape {#sec-pretraining}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number and every code output in the subword
tokenization section was produced by running the code shown, with `tiktoken`
0.13, `sentencepiece` 0.2.2 and `tokenizers` 0.22; the full environment is in
@sec-setup. The BPE tool in that section and the tokenizer-budget and scaling
calculators on this page are interactive.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- draw the stages (pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, preference tuning)
  that turn a randomly initialised transformer first into a base model and then
  into an instruction-tuned assistant, and say what data and what objective
  each stage uses;
- follow a token from a web crawl into a training batch, naming what each
  filtering step removes and what it is protecting against;
- explain why the most aggressive deduplication in an open dataset made the
  data *worse*, and what that tells you about quality filters in general;
- estimate a pretraining run's compute roughly from its parameter and token
  counts, work out the elapsed time and rental cost separately from an assumed
  GPU utilisation, and state where that estimate stops being true;
- read model FLOPs utilization as the gap between a hardware brochure and a
  datacentre, and attribute the gap to the right cause;
- explain how byte-pair encoding (BPE) works, and use a given set of starting
  units and merge rules to work out how a new word is split into tokens;
- measure what a tokenizer costs a language, and price that cost in context
  window, in latency, and in money;
- classify a model release by what it actually opens — weights, data, code,
  licence — and choose one for a task and a budget.

## A model that can compute and knows nothing

At the end of @sec-transformers we had a machine with the right shape and no
contents. Every matrix in it — $W^Q$, $W^K$, $W^V$, $W_1$, $W_2$, the
embedding table — is full of small random numbers. The architecture is
finished. The model knows nothing. Ask a freshly initialised Llama-shaped
network to continue *kedi sütü* and, because standard small initialisation
leaves the scores close together, it hands back a token drawn roughly uniformly
from 128,000 possibilities — meaningless as language.

Everything the model will ever know arrives through one procedure, repeated a
few million times:

> show it a stretch of text, ask it to predict the next token, measure how
> wrong it was, and nudge every parameter slightly in the direction that would
> have made the true token more likely.

That is pretraining's mechanism; there is no second one. Grammar, the capital
of France, how to close a Python bracket, the fact that coffee can be ready and
robots take instructions — all of it arrives as a side effect of getting better
at that one prediction, over enough text; how much of it arrives depends on the
data, the architecture and the optimisation choices.

::: {.column-margin}
Next-token prediction is the objective of *decoder-only* models such as GPT
and Llama, the family this chapter follows. The encoder models of
@sec-model-families use variants of the same idea. BERT (and BERTurk, which
appears in the tokenizer table below) hides about 15% of the tokens and
predicts them from both sides: *masked language modelling*. T5 hides whole
spans of text and generates them: *span corruption*. The recipe is the same —
hide some text, predict it, measure the error.
:::

[This chapter is about what happens when you run that loop at industrial
scale.]{.hl} Where the text comes from, what has to be thrown away before it
is usable, what the run costs in hardware and hours and money, why a Turkish
sentence can cost more than its English translation, and how to tell model
releases apart by what they share and what their model cards show, rather than
by their announcements.

### Three stages, and the first one dominates the data bill

A deployable assistant is not the output of one training run. It is the output
of a short pipeline, and [the stages differ in what they are *for*, not just
in how much data they consume]{.hl}.

The two things that matter about each stage are *what the data is* and *how
much of it there is*, and they point in opposite directions: the stage with
the most data has the least curation, and the stage with the most careful
curation has almost no data.
:::
::::

Put published numbers on that gap. GPT-3 was pretrained on 300 billion tokens
[@brown2020language]. The InstructGPT work that turned a GPT-3-class base
model into something you could talk to used about 13,000 supervised prompts —
12,725 in the training split, averaging 408 tokens each, so on the order of
five million tokens of prompt text — plus 33,000 prompts for the reward model
and 31,000 for the reinforcement-learning stage [@ouyang2022training].

[Pretraining saw roughly 58,000 times the *prompt* tokens that supervised
fine-tuning did.]{.hl} Read the denominator carefully: those five million tokens
are prompts only, and an SFT example is a prompt plus a response, with the loss
usually taken on the response. The ratio against the complete training text is
smaller, and neither paper reports it.

Even so, the order of magnitude is the most useful single fact about this
pipeline, because it explains a pattern you would otherwise find baffling: a
fine-tune often changes *how* a model answers strongly, and usually moves *what
it knows* more modestly (how much depends on the data, the method and the
evaluation). Facts *can* be taught later, and @sec-post-training
measures both effects. But a few million tokens against three hundred billion
is not the place to install a worldview, and retrieval is usually the easier
way to keep facts current. The bulk of the knowledge was installed in stage 1. Stages 2 and 3 are, as an
analogy, close to a coat of paint — an important one, applied by skilled people,
on a building someone else spent tens of millions of dollars constructing.

::: {.column-margin}
The word *pretraining* is a historical accident. It was coined when the stage
really was preliminary: you pretrained on unlabelled text, then trained
properly on your labelled task. Today this first stage usually consumes the
most data and compute, and the name never caught up.
:::

This chapter is about stage 1. @sec-post-training takes stages 2 and 3
seriously, including LoRA, DPO, and what "alignment" actually buys.

### Why the order cannot be swapped

It is worth being explicit about why you cannot skip to stage 2, since stage 2
is the one whose data you can actually afford.

The instruction data is far too small to teach a language.

Five million tokens is roughly forty novels. We would not expect a model
trained from scratch to reach an assistant's command of English syntax — let
alone Python semantics and the geography of Anatolia — from forty novels. A
model can certainly learn *something* from a corpus that size; broad general
competence is not what we would expect it to acquire there, and a model with
billions of parameters runs a high risk of mostly memorising them.

What five million carefully written tokens *can* do is teach a **format**.
That a question is followed by an answer rather than by another question. That
a request for a list produces a list. That *"I don't know"* is a permitted
output.

And format is cheap to learn precisely because the
[base model](#gloss-base-model){#term-base-model .term-ref} already has every ingredient. It simply had no reason to
prefer one arrangement over another.

::: {#gloss-base-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**base model** — what pretraining produces on its own: something that continues text plausibly, with no particular reason to answer a question rather than ask another one. [↩](#term-base-model){.term-back}
:::

That is the cause and effect worth carrying. The table has a fourth row that
the three-stage picture above leaves out; the paragraph after the table
explains it.

| stage | supplies | costs | can it be redone? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| pretraining | knowledge, grammar, world model | weeks to months for a large model, thousands of GPUs | for most teams, in practice no; rarely, with a large budget |
| fine-tuning | format, task shape, domain style | hours to days depending on data and model, often one node | often |
| preference tuning | tone, refusals, ranking of answers | days, plus annotation and candidate generation | usually per release |
| RL on verifiable rewards | reasoning traces, tool use | days to weeks, a real cluster | depends on infrastructure and budget |

**A fourth stage arrived after that picture was drawn.** Since late 2024, models
trained for reasoning add large-scale reinforcement learning against verifiable
rewards — maths with a checkable answer, code with a passing test — and that
stage does not fit the "coat of paint" description. Its token counts stay small,
but its *compute* does not: rollouts are generation, and generation is the
expensive half of RL. The 58,000× ratio above is a fact about **data**, not
about **dollars**, and @sec-reasoning is where the dollars go.

The last column is why this chapter matters even if you never train anything.
[The pretraining decisions are the ones you inherit and that are expensive to
undo.]{.hl} If the tokenizer splits Turkish badly, every user of that model pays
for it; changing the tokenizer means re-adapting the model.
If the data cutoff is December 2023, later training *can* teach the model who
won an election in 2025 — you then own the coverage, the reliability and the
interference, which is why retrieval usually wins for facts that keep moving.
If the corpus contained little Turkish, an adapter has little to build on; how
much that limits the result has to be measured on the target task.

**What we will look at.** What pretraining produces and — more usefully —
what it does not. Then the three decisions that consume the budget before any
architecture question arrives: where the text comes from, how it is cut into
tokens, and what the run actually costs. We finish with the landscape of
models you can choose from, and how to read a claim about one.

## Where the data comes from {#sec-pretraining-data}

The honest answer to "what is a large language model trained on?" is: the web,
plus whatever else the lab could obtain, minus an enormous amount that had to
be thrown away during text extraction, language selection, quality filtering
and deduplication. The interesting part is the *minus*: what each step removes,
and why.

### The raw material

Most open pretraining corpora begin at [Common Crawl](#gloss-common-crawl){#term-common-crawl .term-ref}, a nonprofit
that has crawled the web since 2008 and publishes the results. It releases a
*snapshot* every month or two; the FineWeb team worked from 96 of them
[@penedo2024fineweb]. A snapshot is on the order of hundreds of terabytes of raw
HTTP responses, varying with the period and the file type downloaded.

::: {#gloss-common-crawl .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Common Crawl** — a nonprofit that has crawled the public web since 2008 and publishes each crawl free of charge. Most open pretraining corpora start here. [↩](#term-common-crawl){.term-back}
:::

Two file formats matter, and choosing between them is the first real decision.
WARC files hold the raw crawl response — the full page HTML and the request
metadata. WET files hold Common Crawl's own plain-text extraction; using them
saves a separate extraction step and its compute.
FineWeb used WARC and ran their own extraction with `trafilatura`, for a reason
they state plainly: [the WET files "retained too much boilerplate and menu
text"]{.hl} [@penedo2024fineweb]. Navigation bars, cookie notices, and footer
links are text, and a next-token objective will happily learn to predict them.

This is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through the entire
pipeline: *the model has no way to tell you its data was bad.* It minimises the
loss it is given, and next-token loss does not tell a cookie banner from the
information you want. If cookie banners take up a lot of the corpus, part of the
training budget goes to modelling them — say a tenth of the achievable loss
reduction lives there, and the model gets good at cookie banners. What that
share really is has to be measured on the data.

### What each filter is actually protecting against

A list of filters is boring. The reason each one exists is not.

| filter | removes | the failure it prevents |
|:--|:--|:--|
| URL blocklist | pages on an adult-content list | training on material you cannot defend and cannot later remove |
| `trafilatura` extraction | navigation, ads, footers | a model fluent in "Accept all cookies" |
| fastText language ID, score $\ge 0.65$ | pages not confidently English | a corpus whose claimed language is not its actual language |
| repetition filters | pages that repeat one line 400 times | degenerate loops at generation time |
| quality heuristics | no terminal punctuation, absurd symbol ratios | keyword-stuffed spam no human ever read |
| MinHash deduplication | near-identical documents | memorisation, and compute spent twice on one text |
| PII reformatting | e-mail addresses, public IP addresses | a model that can be prompted into leaking a real person's details |

Two of those rows deserve more than a table cell.

**Deduplication earns its place empirically.** Models trained on deduplicated
data memorise their training set substantially less, and are no worse
downstream [@lee2022deduplicating]. The memorisation is not hypothetical:
given the right prompt, a large model will emit long verbatim passages of its
training data, including personal information [@carlini2021extracting].
Duplicates make this worse for a mechanical reason — a passage that appears a
hundred times is a passage the gradient has rewarded the model a hundred times
for reproducing.

**The language filter is a policy, not a measurement.** A 0.65 threshold on an
English classifier does not merely *detect* language, it *defines* the corpus.
Code-switched text, Turkish written without diacritics, English with heavy
dialect features: all score lower, all get dropped. When a model is later found
weak on some variety of language, this is usually where it happened — silently,
months before anybody trained anything.

### The deduplication surprise

Now the result that should change how you think about data pipelines.

[Deduplication](#gloss-deduplication){#term-deduplication .term-ref} has an obvious knob: how widely do you look for
duplicates? Within one snapshot, or across all 96? Across all of them is more
thorough, so it ought to be better.

::: {#gloss-deduplication .column-margin .term-gloss}
**deduplication** — removing documents that are identical or near-identical to ones already kept, so the model does not spend compute on, or memorise, the same text repeatedly. [↩](#term-deduplication){.term-back}
:::

FineWeb tried exactly that. The two strategies are alternative routes from the
same starting point: run on the ~36 trillion tokens of base-filtered text,
per-snapshot deduplication leaves **20 trillion** and global deduplication
leaves **4 trillion** — a fifth as much, and roughly a ninth of what went in.
It also hit the oldest snapshots hardest, [removing "as much as 90% of the
original base filtered data"]{.hl} from them, since those had 95 later crawls
to be deduplicated against [@penedo2024fineweb].

Then they checked, which is the part most pipelines skip. Taking the 2013-48
snapshot in isolation, they built two *pools*: the ~31 billion tokens global
deduplication had **kept**, and 171 billion tokens re-deduplicated out of the
~460 billion it had **removed**. They then trained one ablation model on a
sample from each pool, at the same model size and the same token budget, so the
only variable was which pool the tokens came from. The kept pool lost.

That equal-budget detail is what makes the result mean anything. Had one model
simply seen more tokens than the other, the comparison would have measured data
*quantity* and told you nothing about data *quality*, which is the whole claim.

Their explanation, after reading documents by hand, is what to memorise: the
data surviving aggressive global deduplication "contains more ads, incoherent
lists of keywords and generally badly formatted text than originally removed
data" [@penedo2024fineweb].

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Why this happens, and why it will happen to you.** The mechanism is worth
getting right, because the obvious explanation is wrong. Deduplication does
not throw away good writing — it keeps one copy of everything. What matters is
*which* copy it keeps. FineWeb deduplicated iteratively, starting from the
newest snapshot and working backwards, so every document that also appeared in
a later crawl was struck from the older ones. Good writing is exactly what gets
quoted, syndicated and mirrored forward in time, so it survives in the recent
snapshots and is stripped from the old ones. Spam is generated fresh and never
reappears, so it stays where it was.

Nothing good was deleted. But within any one old snapshot the *proportion* of
junk went up, and the paper says so directly: [global deduplication "upsamples
lower-quality data in the last deduplicated crawl, resulting in worse
performance of the retained data compared to the removed data"]{.hl}
[@penedo2024fineweb].

The general lesson: a proxy — here, duplication — was standing in for something
you actually wanted, and past a certain strength the proxy inverted. Nobody
would have caught this by reasoning about it. They caught it by training two
models and comparing.
:::

This is why FineWeb deduplicates *within* each snapshot and stops there. It is
also a preview of an argument that recurs throughout this book: when a data
decision looks obviously right, the cost of checking it with a small training
run is almost always lower than the cost of being wrong at scale.

### Quantity is not weight

Having collected data, you must decide how much of each kind the model
actually sees. These are different numbers, and conflating them is a classic
misreading of a model report.

GPT-3's table makes the distinction unusually clear [@brown2020language]:

| dataset | tokens available | share of the training mix | times seen in 300B tokens |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Common Crawl (filtered) | 410B | 60% | 0.44 |
| WebText2 | 19B | 22% | 2.9 |
| Books1 | 12B | 8% | 1.9 |
| Books2 | 55B | 8% | 0.43 |
| Wikipedia | 3B | 3% | 3.4 |

Read the last two columns together. Wikipedia is **0.6%** of the available
tokens and **3%** of the training mix, so the model went through the whole of
Wikipedia 3.4 times while reading less than half of the filtered web crawl.
The authors say why in one sentence: the weights are deliberately *not*
proportional to size, and they accept "a small amount of overfitting in
exchange for higher quality training data" [@brown2020language].

Two bookkeeping notes before you reuse this table. The mix column is the
paper's own rounded figures and sums to 101%, not 100%. And the last column is
the paper's reported epoch count, not something you can recompute from the
other two: share × 300B ÷ tokens available gives 3.5 for WebText2 against the
2.9 printed, and 3.0 for Wikipedia against the 3.4 printed. These are the
figures the original table reports; they do not reconcile exactly, and rounded
shares are not enough to establish why. Read the table for the *shape* of the
argument — quantity
is not weight — and not as a set of numbers that close.

Four years later Llama 3 reports its mixture by *topic* rather than by source,
which itself tells you what the field learned to care about: roughly [50%
general knowledge, 25% mathematical and reasoning tokens, 17% code, and 8%
multilingual]{.hl} [@grattafiori2024llama3]. Note the last figure. Eight
percent, shared across every language that is not English, in a model
explicitly marketed as multilingual. Keep that number — it returns when we
price what Turkish costs.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Code is not in there for the coding.** Seventeen percent of a
general-purpose model's diet being source code looks odd until you consider
what code *is*: long-range structured text in which a mistake thousands of
tokens earlier makes the continuation invalid. It is the most reliably
self-checking text on the internet. Whether it is *causally* responsible for
better reasoning is still argued; that labs keep raising the proportion tells
you what they believe.
:::

### The last forty million tokens

Llama 3's pretraining is itself three stages, and the proportions are
startling [@grattafiori2024llama3]:

1. **Initial pretraining.** AdamW, peak learning rate $8\times10^{-5}$, warmed
   up over 8,000 steps, decayed on a cosine schedule to $8\times10^{-7}$ over
   1.2 million steps. The batch size *grows*: 4M tokens at sequence length
   4,096, doubled to 8M tokens at length 8,192 after 252M tokens, doubled
   again to 16M after 2.87 trillion tokens. Small batches early buy stability;
   large batches later buy efficiency.
2. **Long-context pretraining.** The context window is raised from 8K to 128K
   in six stages, using roughly 800 billion tokens — about 5% of the whole run
   spent purely on learning to use a longer window.
3. **Annealing.** Over the **final 40 million tokens** the learning rate is
   taken linearly to zero while the data mix shifts to upsample very
   high-quality sources. The released weights are then a Polyak average of
   checkpoints from this phase.

Forty million tokens is $0.00026\%$ of 15.6 trillion. Can so little matter?
The paper tested this in a separate experiment, not on the final 40M-token
stage itself. Taking a pre-trained 8B model through an
[annealing](#gloss-annealing){#term-annealing .term-ref} phase on a mix that
upweighted high-quality code and mathematics (including the GSM8k and MATH
*training* sets) improved its GSM8k score by 24.0% and MATH by 6.4%. On the
405B model the same treatment made a negligible difference, which the authors
read as the larger model already having the capability and not needing the
reminder.

::: {#gloss-annealing .column-margin .term-gloss}
**annealing** — taking the learning rate down to zero at the end of a run, usually while shifting the data mix toward the best material available. Borrowed from metallurgy, where slow cooling settles a structure. [↩](#term-annealing){.term-back}
:::

[Where a token sits in the schedule changes what it teaches.]{.hl} A token
seen at step 400,000 under a large learning rate contributes to a broad
capability that the remaining 800,000 updates will partly overwrite. A token seen
in the last 0.00026% of the run, as the learning rate goes to zero, lands in
weights that will never move again. That mechanism is behind an otherwise
mysterious industrial habit: save the best data for last.

### How many times may you reuse a token?

Sooner or later every serious pretraining project runs out of the language it
wants. This is already true for Turkish, and it will be true for English
sooner than the raw token counts suggest. The obvious move is more epochs (complete passes over the training data) over
what you have.

The measured answer is more generous than folklore expects
[@muennighoff2023scaling]. Training on [up to four epochs of repeated data
"yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data"]{.hl}. Past
that, the value of each further epoch decays — and eventually the value of
adding *compute* decays to zero as well, because extra passes over data the
model has already exhausted cannot help.

The practical shape of the advice:

| your situation | what the evidence supports |
|:--|:--|
| more unique tokens than your compute can use | use unique data; never repeat |
| data-limited, modest compute overrun | repeat up to about 4 epochs, nearly free |
| data-limited, large compute overrun | split it between parameters *and* epochs, tilting toward epochs |
| far past both limits | stop; the extra compute is buying nothing |

The third row is the one that surprises people, so take it from the authors
directly: in the data-constrained regime, [allocating new compute to "both more
parameters and epochs is necessary, and … epochs should be scaled slightly
faster"]{.hl} [@muennighoff2023scaling]. Their figure puts it more sharply
still — the data suggest "training smaller models for more epochs, in contrast
to what assuming Chinchilla scaling laws hold for repeated data would predict".
If you reach for Chinchilla's ratio when you are short of data, it will tell
you to buy parameters, and it will be wrong.

For a Turkish project this is genuinely liberating. A corpus of 30 billion
Turkish tokens does not cap you at 30 billion tokens of training; it is closer
to 120 billion before returns visibly bend, which changes what model size is
defensible.

## Subword tokenization: how a model sees text {#sec-subword}

@sec-text-as-data cut text into words and counted them; for bag-of-words and
TF-IDF that was enough. A pretrained language model does not see text as words.
It sees the units its own tokenizer produces, and those are usually smaller
than a word. That is what "token" meant all through @sec-transformers, where we
did not ask where the tokens came from.

This section answers that question. First we build BPE step by step on a small
corpus. Then we look at what changes when the starting alphabet is characters
or bytes, and at why the same tokenizer cuts a Turkish text into more tokens
than its English counterpart. WordPiece, which BERT uses, and Unigram LM, which
T5 uses, are two relatives of the same idea; the "Deep dive" boxes at the end
of the section run them, and @sec-tokenizer-algorithms compares them alongside
the models. The section after this one (@sec-tokenizer-budget) prices the same
decision as a budget line at pretraining scale.

### Subwords: the compromise that won {#sec-text-as-data-bpe}

::: {#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .column-margin .term-gloss}
**byte-pair encoding (BPE)** — a way of learning the token list from the
text itself: start from single characters (or bytes), and keep gluing together
whichever pair occurs most often. [↩](#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){.term-back}
:::

With word-level tokenization, a fixed vocabulary may not cover every word form
met in new text. Character-level tokenization usually represents the same text
with longer sequences, and the model has to learn word pieces and words from
those small units. [Byte-pair encoding]{.hl}
([BPE](#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .term-ref}) offers an option between the two by *learning* its units from data
[@sennrich2016neural].

See the three options on one word. Suppose `unbreakable` never appeared in the
tokenizer's training text. In the comparison we assume that the word-level
tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary and writes `<UNK>` (unknown) for words it does
not know. The character-level tokenizer's alphabet contains every character of
the word.

| Unit | How `unbreakable` looks | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Word | `<UNK>` | The whole word is not in the vocabulary, so its spelling is not kept; the unknown-word marker takes its place. |
| Character | `u` `n` `b` `r` `e` `a` `k` `a` `b` `l` `e` | The spelling of the word is kept, in eleven units. The model learns the patterns inside the word from the order of those units. |
| Subword | `un` `break` `able` | The word is represented with three units. These pieces occur in other words too: `undo`, `breaking`, `readable`. |

: One word at three unit sizes {tbl-colwidths="[16,34,50]"}

The split in the last row is not made up: OpenAI's `cl100k_base` tokenizer cuts
this word exactly there. Which leaves a question: who chose `un`, `break` and
`able`? Nobody did. They were found by counting.

In this example BPE training starts by splitting the words into characters. To
each word we append `</w>`, a symbol that marks the end of a word. We count
adjacent pairs of symbols, weighting each word by its frequency in the corpus,
and merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol. Then we update the counts
and repeat. The code below makes ten merges. Which of several equally frequent
pairs is chosen first depends on the implementation; this code takes the first
one it met.

```python
from collections import Counter

corpus = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
words = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): n for w, n in corpus.items()}

def pair_counts(words):
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def merge(words, pair):
    a, b = pair
    out = {}
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        new, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                new.append(a + b)
                i += 2
            else:
                new.append(symbols[i])
                i += 1
        out[tuple(new)] = freq
    return out

merges = []
for step in range(1, 11):
    best, count = pair_counts(words).most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(best)
    words = merge(words, best)
    print(f"merge {step:>2}: {best[0]!r} + {best[1]!r} -> "
          f"{best[0] + best[1]!r}  (seen {count} times)")
```

```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```

The first two merges build `est`, which in these words coincides with the
English superlative suffix. The third merges it with the end-of-word marker:
`est</w>`. Later steps build `low` and `new` as well. [The algorithm does not
recognise these pieces as stems or suffixes; at each step it picks the most
frequent adjacent pair of symbols.]{.hl} In this small corpus it helps that
some pieces coincide with morphemes, but BPE does not guarantee that they will.

BPE can also split words that are not in the tokenizer's training corpus into
learned pieces. To tokenize a new word in this example, we apply the merge
rules in the order they were learned:

```python
def apply_merges(word, merges):
    symbols = tuple(word) + ("</w>",)
    for pair in merges:
        symbols = tuple(merge({symbols: 1}, pair).keys())[0]
    return symbols

for w in ["lowest", "newer", "slow", "widest"]:
    print(f"{w:<8} -> {' '.join(apply_merges(w, merges))}")
```

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

`lowest` is not in the tokenizer's training corpus, and yet it is represented
with two units from the vocabulary: `low` and `est</w>`. This is the main
reason subwords became common: **in this BPE setup, as long as the characters
of the starting alphabet remain available, a word never seen before can still
be built from those characters and their learned merges.** Some pieces, like
the `s` in `slow`, can stay single characters. Using smaller pieces can raise
the number of tokens; how that affects a language model's performance has to
be evaluated separately.

Notice the condition: every *character* of the new word has to be in the
alphabet the merges were learned over. Ours came from four English words. What
happens when a letter outside it arrives, a `ç` for instance?
@sec-text-as-data-bytes takes that up after the figure.

//| echo: false
// Verbatim output of the merge loop at the top of this section — if the small
// corpus changes, regenerate both together.
bpeMerges = [
  ["e", "s"], ["es", "t"], ["est", "</w>"], ["l", "o"], ["lo", "w"],
  ["n", "e"], ["ne", "w"], ["new", "est</w>"], ["low", "</w>"], ["w", "i"]

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bpeTrace = {
  const raw = bpeWord || "";
  const alphabet = new Set("deilnorstw");
  const invalid = [...new Set([...raw].filter(c => !alphabet.has(c)))];

  const trace = [];
  trace.invalid = invalid;
  if (!raw.length || invalid.length) return trace;

  let symbols = [...raw, "</w>"];
  trace.push({ step: 0, rule: "start (characters)", symbols: [...symbols] });
  bpeMerges.forEach(([a, b], k) => {
    const out = [];
    let i = 0, used = false;
    while (i < symbols.length) {
      if (i < symbols.length - 1 && symbols[i] === a && symbols[i + 1] === b) {
        out.push(a + b); i += 2; used = true;
      } else { out.push(symbols[i]); i += 1; }
    }
    symbols = out;
    if (used) trace.push({ step: k + 1, rule: `${a} + ${b}`, symbols: [...symbols] });
  });
  return trace;
}
```

### Characters or bytes: what BPE starts from {#sec-text-as-data-bytes}

The example above started from characters. Tokenizers that use byte-level BPE,
such as GPT-2's and `cl100k_base`, start from bytes. To see the difference, we
explain the terms character, code point, character encoding and byte through
ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8.

A **character** is an abstract unit that text is made of; letters, digits,
punctuation marks and spaces are examples. `ç`, `a`, `y`, `7`, `?` and `😀`
are visible ones. But a unit perceived as a single sign on screen can be
represented in Unicode by one code point or by several.

Computers store text as sequences of bits. A character encoding determines how
the units of text are represented by those sequences. **ASCII** is a 7-bit
character encoding whose first version was published in 1963. Its 128 code
values cover the English letters, the digits, punctuation, the space and
control characters. The code value of the letter `a` is 97. ASCII has no `ç`,
`ş` or `ğ`, no Arabic or Chinese script, and no emoji.

**Unicode** is the standard that aims to represent the characters of different
writing systems in one shared system. The numerical positions in Unicode's code
space are called **code points**; encoded characters are assigned to them. A
code point is usually written as `U+` followed by the number in hexadecimal:
the code point of `ç` is 231, that is U+00E7. The 128 ASCII characters keep
their numbers in Unicode, so `a` is still 97.

A **byte** is the basic unit a computer stores data in. It is eight bits and
holds a number from 0 to 255, so it can take only 256 different values.
Unicode's numbers go far beyond 255, so a code point does not always fit in
one byte. An *encoding* decides which bytes store a code point. **UTF-8**,
which is widely used on the web, represents every encodable Unicode code point
with one to four bytes. Code points in the ASCII range are encoded as a single
byte, and larger values as two, three or four bytes, using bit patterns that
UTF-8 defines.

Here are all three side by side on the Turkish word `çay` (tea):

| | `ç` | `a` | `y` |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Unicode code point | 231 (U+00E7) | 97 (U+0061) | 121 (U+0079) |
| In the ASCII table? | no | yes | yes |
| UTF-8 bytes | 195, 167 | 97 | 121 |

: `çay`: three code points, and four bytes in UTF-8, when `ç` is written as U+00E7 {tbl-colwidths="[34,24,21,21]"}

In this spelling `çay` is three letters and three code points, and takes four
bytes when encoded in UTF-8. In Python `len("çay")` is 3 and
`len("çay".encode("utf-8"))` is 4. Text that looks the same can also be written
with a different sequence of code points: write `c` followed by a separate
cedilla mark instead of `ç`, and the same word is four code points and five
bytes. These numbers depend on the Unicode spelling and on the encoding.

Why does a tokenizer care? Because the symbols BPE starts merging from are
either characters or bytes, and there are very different *numbers* of each:

- **A character alphabet can be large.** Unicode's code space is finite, but it
  holds a great many characters, and new versions define new ones. A
  tokenizer's starting alphabet can be chosen from the training data;
  characters can be added to it, or its coverage limited. A character that is
  not in that alphabet needs an extra mechanism, such as an unknown token or a
  fallback to bytes.
- **A byte alphabet can be complete with 256 values.** If the starting alphabet
  contains every byte value, every byte of UTF-8 encoded text can be
  represented. The bytes of a new character then need no new starting symbol.

The rest of this section works through the two options and what each costs.

First a short note on history. The loop above — count adjacent pairs, merge the
most frequent, repeat — *is* BPE. The name is older than its use in NLP: it comes from a 1994 data-compression
algorithm that kept replacing the most frequent pair of adjacent **bytes** in a
file with a single byte value the file did not use [@gage1994new]. Sennrich and
colleagues kept the loop and changed its purpose: the merges build a vocabulary
instead of shrinking a file, and the merge list is kept so it can be replayed
on new text [@sennrich2016neural].

That leaves one decision the loop does not make for you: **what the starting
symbols are**. Do not confuse it with the choice of algorithm; the two are
separate decisions. BPE is not the only way to learn a subword vocabulary. You
will meet two relatives of it later: **WordPiece**, which BERT uses, and
**Unigram**, which T5 uses. All three are used to build subword vocabularies,
but they differ in how the vocabulary is learned and in how new text is split
into pieces. Our main example here is BPE. WordPiece and Unigram come up in a
"Deep dive" box in this chapter (@sec-text-as-data-granularities), and the
methods are compared in more detail where we look at BERT's tokenizer
(@sec-tokenizer-algorithms). What you need for now:
the algorithm decides *how* units are learned. Characters or bytes decide *what
they are built from*, and that question is the same for all three algorithms.

**Starting from characters.** This is what the example above did. The merge
table can only combine symbols it has seen, and the alphabet this one saw came
from four English words. `apply_merges("çay", merges)` returns
`('ç', 'a', 'y', '</w>')`. But `ç`, `a` and `y` are not in the starting
alphabet built from this small corpus. The function only applies merge rules
and does not check for symbols outside the vocabulary, so it leaves them in the
output. A usable tokenizer has to handle this case separately: it can add the
characters to its starting alphabet, use an unknown token (`<UNK>`), or fall
back to bytes. That a character is rare does not mean it must become an
unknown token.

**Starting from bytes.** The other option is to start from the UTF-8 bytes of
the characters instead of the characters themselves. UTF-8 represents every
encodable Unicode code point with one to four bytes. ASCII letters take one
byte. In the spellings below, each of the Turkish letters `ç`, `ş`, `ğ`, `ı`,
`ö`, `ü` and `İ` is two bytes; `世` is three and `😀` is four. Emoji and other
combined spellings made of more than one code point can be longer than four
bytes in total:

```python
for ch in ["a", "ç", "ş", "İ", "世", "😀"]:
    b = ch.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{ch}  U+{ord(ch):04X}  {len(b)} byte(s): {' '.join(f'{x:02X}' for x in b)}")
```

```text
a  U+0061  1 byte(s): 61
ç  U+00E7  2 byte(s): C3 A7
ş  U+015F  2 byte(s): C5 9F
İ  U+0130  2 byte(s): C4 B0
世  U+4E16  3 byte(s): E4 B8 96
😀  U+1F600  4 byte(s): F0 9F 98 80
```

A byte has only 256 possible values, so an alphabet of 256 bytes is closed:
every string in every language is a sequence of them. Byte-level BPE runs
exactly the same merge loop over byte sequences instead of characters
[@radford2019language]. At each step the loop merges the most frequent
adjacent pair of symbols. Some characters and word pieces can end up
represented as single tokens that way. The two bytes of `ç`, for example, can
become one token; whether that happens, and at which step, depends on the
frequencies in the training data and on the number of merges made.
But [the merges are not bound to Unicode character boundaries]{.hl}: the
algorithm does not know where a character ends, only which byte pair is
frequent. So a token can stand for a whole character, for several characters,
or for only part of one UTF-8 character. The next output shows all three.

Here is a byte-level tokenizer, OpenAI's `cl100k_base`, showing the bytes behind
each token. `enc.encode` returns the token ids as a list of integers. Text is
passed to the model through those ids. `decode_single_token_bytes` shows the
sequence of bytes each id stands for:

```python
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
for text in ["çay", "şişe", "ŞİŞE", "😀"]:
    pieces = [enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t) for t in enc.encode(text)]
    print(f"{text:<5} {len(pieces)} tokens  {pieces}")
```

```text
çay   2 tokens  [b'\xc3\xa7', b'ay']
şişe  3 tokens  [b'\xc5\x9fi', b'\xc5\x9f', b'e']
ŞİŞE  6 tokens  [b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'\xc4\xb0', b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'E']
😀     2 tokens  [b'\xf0\x9f\x98', b'\x80']
```

In this output the two bytes of `ç` sit in a single token. `ŞİŞE` produces six
tokens and `şişe` three. The two bytes of capital `Ş` are split over separate
tokens, while `İ` and `E` stay whole. From this output alone we cannot tell how
often `Ş` occurred in the training data. `b'\xc5'` is not a valid UTF-8
sequence on its own; it has to be joined with the next byte before the
character can be read. `😀` is split into two tokens as well: the first holds
three bytes and the second the last one. None of these examples needs an
unknown token; but the same number of visible characters can produce different
numbers of tokens.

In the table below, "character" means a Unicode code point. The byte-level
column assumes that the starting alphabet contains all 256 byte values.

| | BPE starting from characters | BPE starting from bytes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Starting alphabet | Selected code points; they can be taken from the training data or added separately. | The 256 byte values. |
| A character that is not in the starting alphabet | [Needs an extra mechanism, such as an unknown token or the byte fallback below.]{.con} | [Represented by its UTF-8 bytes.]{.pro} |
| What does one token stand for? | [One or more whole code points.]{.pro} | [A sequence of bytes; sometimes only part of the UTF-8 form of a code point.]{.con} |
| Cost of a code point that is not merged into a larger piece | [One token, if it is in the alphabet.]{.pro} | [One to four tokens, depending on its UTF-8 form and on the learned merges.]{.con} |
| Coverage | Limited to the chosen alphabet and to the fallback mechanism, if there is one. | Covers every byte of UTF-8 encoded text. |

: Characters or bytes as the starting alphabet {tbl-colwidths="[26,37,37]"}

A third design combines the two: **byte fallback**, which means spelling an
unknown character out in bytes. The vocabulary is still built from characters
and their merges, but one token for each of the 256 byte values is added to it.
The tokenizer handles the characters it knows as usual. When it meets one it
does not know, it writes that character's UTF-8 bytes one by one with those
byte tokens instead of writing `<UNK>`. The SentencePiece library offers this
as an option (`byte_fallback=True`).

A small experiment shows it. Below, SentencePiece is trained twice on eight
Turkish words that contain no `ç`: once with the option off and once with it
on. Both models are then given the word `çay`:

```python
import sentencepiece as spm

words = ["ev", "evde", "evden", "evler", "yol", "yolda", "yoldan", "yollar"]
with open("mini.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(words * 5) + "\n")            # no 'ç' anywhere in this text

for fallback in [False, True]:
    spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
        input="mini.txt", model_prefix="mini", model_type="bpe",
        vocab_size=20 + (256 if fallback else 0), byte_fallback=fallback,
        character_coverage=1.0, hard_vocab_limit=False, minloglevel=2,
        bos_id=-1, eos_id=-1, pad_id=-1)
    sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file="mini.model")
    ids = sp.encode("çay")
    print(f"byte_fallback={fallback!s:<5}  vocabulary {sp.get_piece_size():>3}  "
          f"{sp.encode('çay', out_type=str)}  ->  {sp.decode(ids)!r}")
```

```text
byte_fallback=False  vocabulary  20  ['▁', 'ç', 'a', 'y']  ->  ' ⁇ ay'
byte_fallback=True   vocabulary 276  ['▁', '<0xC3>', '<0xA7>', 'a', 'y']  ->  'çay'
```

In the first line `ç` is not in the vocabulary and is encoded with the unknown
token's id. The list of pieces still shows `ç`, because that list prints the
unknown piece as it is spelled in the text. It does not mean the vocabulary has
an entry for `ç`. When the ids are turned back into text, a `⁇` mark takes the
letter's place.

In the second line the vocabulary has grown from 20 to 276 with the 256 added
byte tokens. `ç` is represented as `<0xC3>` and `<0xA7>`. Those are the two
bytes from the table above: hexadecimal C3 is 195 and A7 is 167. Turned back
into text from the ids, `çay` comes out intact. The leading `▁` is the mark
SentencePiece uses to make a space visible. Here it stands for the space that
the default setting adds in front of the text; the next section comes back to
this notation.

**Which one is used today.** Many GPT-type models use byte-level BPE or a
variant of it. Other model families also use WordPiece and Unigram.
SentencePiece is a library that can train a tokenizer with either BPE or
Unigram. GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE with a
50,257-token vocabulary [@radford2019language]. OpenAI's `cl100k_base` and
`o200k_base`, measured in the next section, are byte-level. Llama 3 moved to a
128K-token vocabulary that combines 100K tokens from OpenAI's `tiktoken` with 28K
added for non-English languages [@grattafiori2024llama3]. BERT and its close
relatives such as DistilBERT and ELECTRA still ship WordPiece over characters
[@devlin2019bert] (RoBERTa, although built on BERT, switched to GPT-2's
byte-level BPE), and a later
table (@sec-tokenizer-algorithms) shows which algorithm ships where. The
practical rule does not depend on any of this: use the tokenizer the model was
trained with, and count tokens with it.

Coverage and token count have to be kept apart here. If the starting alphabet
contains all 256 byte values, no unknown token is needed to represent the bytes
of a Turkish word encoded in UTF-8. That does not mean the normalization that
runs before tokenization preserves the original text: letters it changed or
spaces it deleted cannot be brought back by byte coverage.

How many tokens a text produces depends on the training data, the learned
merges, and the size and content of the vocabulary. No separate vocabulary
quota needs to have been set for each language. The next section measures this
difference in token counts on Turkish examples.

**This section in short.** The coverage of BPE that starts from characters
depends on the chosen starting alphabet and on extra mechanisms such as byte
fallback, if there are any. BPE that starts from all 256 byte values can
represent the bytes of any UTF-8 encoded text. In return, some code points can
be split over more than one token. In both approaches the number of tokens
depends on the learned vocabulary and on the content of the text.

### Who pays for Turkish {#sec-text-as-data-turkish}

A tokenizer can produce different numbers of tokens for the same content in
different languages. The difference depends on the language mix and the content
of the training corpus, on the vocabulary size, on the tokenization algorithm
and on the preprocessing rules. Let us look at the difference between Turkish
and English on a concrete example. Here is Article 1 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, in the official English and Turkish texts, run
through OpenAI's tokenizers:

```python
import tiktoken

en = ("All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. "
      "They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards "
      "one another in a spirit of brotherhood.")
tr = ("Bütün insanlar hür, haysiyet ve haklar bakımından eşit doğarlar. "
      "Akıl ve vicdana sahiptirler ve birbirlerine karşı kardeşlik "
      "zihniyeti ile hareket etmelidirler.")

for name in ["cl100k_base", "o200k_base"]:
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    a, b = len(enc.encode(en)), len(enc.encode(tr))
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  english : {len(en):>4} code points -> {a:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(en) / a:4.2f} code points/token)")
    print(f"  turkish : {len(tr):>4} code points -> {b:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(tr) / b:4.2f} code points/token)")
    print(f"  Turkish/English token count ratio: {b / a:4.2f}")
```

```text
cl100k_base:
  english :  170 code points ->  33 tokens  (5.15 code points/token)
  turkish :  160 code points ->  60 tokens  (2.67 code points/token)
  Turkish/English token count ratio: 1.82
o200k_base:
  english :  170 code points ->  33 tokens  (5.15 code points/token)
  turkish :  160 code points ->  46 tokens  (3.48 code points/token)
  Turkish/English token count ratio: 1.39
```

In these two-sentence texts of the same article, the Turkish token count is
[about 1.82 times]{.hl} the English one with `cl100k_base`, and 1.39 times with
`o200k_base`. In this example the second encoding narrows the difference.

In a comparison where the same input price per token applies, more tokens mean
a higher input cost. A fixed token limit can also correspond to different
amounts of content in texts like these. The total cost, though, depends on the
model chosen, on the lengths of input and output, and on the pricing terms.

Similar differences between languages have been shown in broader studies
[@petrov2023language]. The two texts here do not give a universal ratio for
Turkish. Nor is it enough to explain the difference by some Turkish letters
taking two bytes in UTF-8; the learned vocabulary and the tokenization rules
act together.

Where does the difference come from? Turkish encodes far more grammatical
information inside a single word, with suffixes, than English does
[@oflazer1994two], so one stem produces many surface forms. English expresses
the same grammatical information with separate words in some constructions. If
those words are frequent in the training corpus, they can be represented with
short token sequences. In Turkish, how the many inflected forms are split
depends on which shared sequences the tokenizer has learned.

Below you can see how the output of `cl100k_base` changes as suffixes are added
to the stem `ev` ("house"). We encoded each word separately, with a single
space in front of it:

```text
ev             1 tokens  [' ev']
evler          2 tokens  [' ev', 'ler']
evlerimiz      4 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz']
evlerimizden   5 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz', 'den']
```
