::: {.fig-cap}
Segmentations produced by running each tokenizer, not by hand. Llama 3's nine
pieces cost 2.25 times what the Turkish-native tokenizer's four do — for one
word, in every forward pass, forever.
:::
::::

Look at where Llama 3 cuts. It splits *bilgisayar* — an ordinary everyday
noun, "computer" — into `bil | gis | ayar`. The word's own parts are *bilgi*
("information") and *sayar* ("counter"), and the cuts ignore that boundary:
`gis` is not a Turkish unit at all, and `ayar` ("setting, adjustment") is an
unrelated real word. The model must reassemble the concept from pieces every
single time it appears.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Fewer tokens is not the same as better linguistics, and the difference
matters.** On *evlerinizden* ("from your houses") Llama 3 produces
`ev | ler | iniz | den` — exactly the four morphemes, a textbook
segmentation. The Turkish-native Cosmos tokenizer produces
`ev | lerinizden`: two tokens, cheaper, and blind to the internal structure,
since `lerinizden` spans three morphemes rather than being one.

So the two metrics genuinely can disagree. Compression is what you pay for
and is easy to measure. Morphological alignment is what might help the model
generalise to a suffix combination it has not seen, and is hard to measure.
Do not assume the cheaper segmentation is the more linguistically sensible
one — check, as we just did.
:::

### BERT's tokenizer: WordPiece and its relatives {#sec-tokenizer-algorithms}

The measurement table has six tokenizers in it, but only two algorithms stand
behind them. GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5 and Cosmos GPT-2 use BPE, the algorithm
this chapter built step by step (@sec-text-as-data-bpe). The two BERT models use
**WordPiece**. A third algorithm that is not in the table, **Unigram LM**, is
the one you will meet in models such as T5 and XLM-R.

All three do the same job: they learn from a corpus which subword pieces go
into the vocabulary. They differ in what they count as a "good" piece. Knowing
which one a model uses is worth it, because that is how you read its output and
predict how it will cut a word.

**Look at the output first.** Run the same word, *evlerinizden* ("from your
houses"), through the two BERT tokenizers and through XLM-R, which uses Unigram
LM:

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

word = "evlerinizden"
for name in ["google-bert/bert-base-multilingual-cased",
             "dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased",
             "FacebookAI/xlm-roberta-base"]:
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
    pieces = tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(tok.encode(word))
    print(f"{name.split('/')[-1]:<30} {' '.join(pieces)}")
```

```text
bert-base-multilingual-cased   [CLS] ev ##lerini ##zde ##n [SEP]
bert-base-turkish-cased        [CLS] evlerini ##z ##den [SEP]
xlm-roberta-base               <s> ▁ev leriniz den </s>
```

BERT's output has two things in it that the GPT family's does not.

**The special tokens at the start and the end.** BERT puts `[CLS]` in front of
every input and `[SEP]` after it. The contextual representation at the `[CLS]`
position is used in tasks such as sentence classification
(@sec-classification). `[SEP]` marks where a text ends, and when the input has
two texts, a question and a passage for instance, one goes between them too.
XLM-R uses `<s>` and `</s>` for similar roles; such markers are not
interchangeable between models.

**The `##` mark.** WordPiece puts `##` in front of every piece that *continues*
a word. A piece without `##` starts a new pre-token. The space GPT keeps
inside a token and the `▁` in XLM-R's output also show how pieces are to be
joined, but the three notations do not carry the same information
(@sec-text-as-data-turkish): `##` does not record how many spaces there were.
One consequence is that `ev` and `##ev` are two separate entries in the
vocabulary; the model learns one vector for `ev` at the start of a word and
another for `ev` inside one. In multilingual BERT's vocabulary of 119,547
entries, 43,606 start with `##`; in BERTurk's 32,000, 7,246 do.

**How WordPiece splits a word.** To split a new word, BPE replays the merges it
learned, in order. WordPiece does not. Its rule is simpler, and it is *greedy*:

- Start at the beginning of the word. Take the **longest** piece that is in the
  vocabulary.
- Do the same for what is left, this time looking for pieces that start with
  `##`.
- Continue until the word is used up.

Follow BERTurk through *evlerinizden*. The vocabulary has `ev`, `evler`,
`evleri` and `evlerini`; it does not have `evleriniz`. So the longest match is
`evlerini`. That leaves `zden`: `##zden` and `##zde` are not in the vocabulary,
`##z` is. That leaves `den`: `##den` is there. Result: `evlerini` `##z` `##den`.

The greedy rule has a cost, and it shows here. The same vocabulary also has
the piece `##lerinizden`, so a two-piece split, `ev` `##lerinizden`, was
possible. Because the rule takes the longest piece at the first step, it never
tries that split and produces three pieces.

**WordPiece can emit `[UNK]`.** If at some point no piece in the vocabulary
matches, WordPiece turns not just that character but the *whole* word into
`[UNK]`. Multilingual BERT's vocabulary has no 😀:

```text
çay 😀    ça ##y [UNK]
çay😀     [UNK]
```

In the second line the emoji was typed directly after the word, and `çay`
(tea) was lost with it. A byte-level BPE tokenizer cannot do this
(@sec-text-as-data-bytes): `cl100k_base` spells the same emoji out in bytes,
as two tokens. So when you work with a BERT-family model, counting the `[UNK]`s
in your input is a cheap and useful check.

**How the three algorithms learn the vocabulary.** So far you have seen how a
finished vocabulary is *used*. How it is *learned* is where the three
algorithms part:

| | What it optimises | Direction | Ships in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BPE** [@sennrich2016neural] | merge the most *frequent* adjacent pair | bottom-up, the vocabulary grows | GPT-2/3/4, RoBERTa, Llama, Gemma |
| **WordPiece** [@schuster2012japanese] | merge the pair that most increases corpus likelihood, roughly maximising $\frac{c(ab)}{c(a)\,c(b)}$ | bottom-up | BERT, DistilBERT, ELECTRA |
| **Unigram LM** [@kudo2018subword] | start from a large candidate set and *prune* the pieces whose removal costs least likelihood, re-estimating piece probabilities by EM (expectation–maximization) | top-down, the vocabulary shrinks | T5, ALBERT, XLNet, XLM-R |

: Three subword algorithms, and what each one is actually maximising
{tbl-colwidths="[16,40,24,20]"}

Read the table row by row, with the intuition for each.

**BPE** merges the pair that occurs side by side most often. Because it rewards
frequency, its vocabulary fills with pieces that many words share: `ler`,
`den`, `lar`.

**WordPiece** does not stop at how often the pair occurs; it divides that count
by how often each of the two parts occurs on its own. That penalises a merge of
two parts that are already very common separately, and favours parts that are
seen almost only together. One caveat about the ratio in the table: BERT's
original training procedure is not published in full. The ratio is the common
approximate reconstruction used to explain its logic.

**Unigram LM** comes from the other direction. It starts with a very large set
of candidate pieces and, in each round, drops the ones whose removal lowers the
likelihood of the corpus least. It can evaluate the alternative splits of a
word with probabilistic scores. In use, the highest-scoring split can be taken,
or one can be sampled from the alternatives. Showing the same text split in
different ways during training is called subword regularization; the aim is to
reduce the model's dependence on a single split [@kudo2018subword]. Its benefit
has to be measured by experiment. Different splits can be produced in a similar
way with BPE-Dropout [@provilkov2020bpe].

One common confusion is worth clearing up here: `SentencePiece`
[@kudo2018sentencepiece] is not a fourth algorithm but a *toolkit* that can run
BPE or Unigram LM. Llama 2 and Gemma use it in BPE mode, T5 and ALBERT in
Unigram mode.

@bostrom2020byte compared Unigram LM with BPE at equal vocabulary size in
English and Japanese experiments. The boundaries of Unigram LM coincided
better with the morphological references used, and models pretrained with that
tokenization did as well as or better than their BPE counterparts on the
downstream tasks evaluated. The findings hold for those experimental
conditions; they do not establish a fixed ranking for all languages and
models.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**If you want to see the three of them run.** The collapsed box "Deep dive:
three ways to learn the same kind of unit" at the end of the subword
tokenization section (@sec-text-as-data-granularities) runs a minimal version
of each on a sixty-word Turkish corpus and has all three split the same two
words.
:::

Now tie this back to the chapter's question. The algorithm explains a small
part of the differences in the measurement table. Multilingual BERT and BERTurk
use the *same* algorithm; one charges Turkish 1.23×, the other 0.58×. What
makes the difference is not the algorithm but the corpus the vocabulary was
trained on.

### What the surcharge actually costs

Take the measured corpus figure for Llama 3: Turkish costs **1.23×** the
tokens of English for identical content. That single number propagates into
four separate bills.

| where it lands | the effect at 1.23× |
|:--|:--|
| context window | a 128,000-token window holds about 104,000 English-equivalent tokens of Turkish |
| API cost | one million English-equivalent tokens costs the price of 1.23 million |
| latency | generation is per token, so at the same tokens-per-second a Turkish answer takes about 23% longer |
| pretraining compute | at fixed FLOPs, a Turkish corpus buys about 19% less content than an English one |

Watch the direction of that last number, because it is the single easiest
mistake to make with a ratio. Turkish costs 1.23× *more* tokens, but a fixed
token budget buys $1/1.23 = 0.813$ of the content — **18.7% less**, not 23%
less. The two are not the same figure, and only the API-cost and latency rows multiply by 1.23; the context-window and compute rows divide by it. That is why
128,000 tokens holds about 104,000 English-equivalent tokens rather than 98,560.

The compute row is the one that compounds. From @sec-scaling-laws, compute
scales with the token count, so a fixed budget spent on Turkish sees roughly a
fifth less *material* than the same budget spent on English — fewer facts,
fewer sentences, fewer patterns, for exactly the same money. The tokenizer tax
is not only charged at inference. It was charged during pretraining, to the
model you are now using.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Measure this for your own language and your own text before you commit.** It
takes about fifteen lines. Take a few hundred sentence pairs of your domain
text and its translation, run every tokenizer you are considering over both
sides, and divide. Domain matters as much as language: legal Turkish, clinical
Turkish, and Turkish social media do not tokenize alike, and a corpus average
will not warn you.
:::

Under 1.23× the pragmatic answer is usually "use the multilingual model
anyway" — 23% is real but it does not overturn a decision. Under GPT-2's
1.98× it does. That is precisely why you measure instead of assuming, and the
full decision, including when a Turkish-native model wins outright, is
@sec-turkish-nlp's subject.

## What a run costs {#sec-pretraining-compute}

You can estimate the compute of any pretraining run — how many
[FLOPs](#gloss-flop){#term-flop .term-ref} it consumed — from two numbers, the
parameter count $N$ and the token count $D$. The estimate counts the weight
matrix multiplies, which dominate the cost of a typical run. The main term it
leaves out is attention; at the short contexts used for most of pretraining
that adds a few to about fifteen percent, and this section comes back to when
it matters more. An estimate this good from two numbers is unusual in systems
work, and it is the tool that lets you sanity-check a press release.

**One caveat first, because it decides which number you put in $N$.** The $6ND$
rule counts operations per parameter *used*, and in a mixture-of-experts model (@sec-moe)
a token only touches the experts its router picked
[@jiang2024mixtral]. So the figure you want is active parameters, not total:

$$C \approx 6\,N_{\text{active}}\,D$$

DeepSeek-V3 makes the gap concrete: 671B total parameters, about 37B active per
token, 14.8T training tokens. Using the active count gives
$6 \times 37{\times}10^{9} \times 14.8{\times}10^{12} \approx 3.3\times10^{24}$
FLOPs; substituting the total would have over-counted by **18×**. Whenever a
release quotes two parameter counts, the smaller one is the one this
arithmetic wants.

::: {#gloss-flop .column-margin .term-gloss}
**FLOP** — one floating-point operation: a single multiply or a single add on numbers stored in floating-point (non-integer) format. Training compute is counted in FLOPs; chips are rated in FLOP/s, operations per second. The two are easy to confuse and differ by a factor of however long you ran. [↩](#term-flop){.term-back}
:::

### Where the 6 comes from

$$
C \;\approx\; 6\,N\,D \quad \text{FLOPs}
$$

The 6 is not a fudge factor. It is three twos, and each two has a cause.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Six floating-point operations per parameter per token</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 320" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="Three panels explaining the constant six. The first panel, the forward pass, costs two operations per parameter per token: one multiply and one add, because every weight is used once in a multiply-accumulate. The second panel, the backward pass computing gradients with respect to the layer input so the error can travel further back, costs another two. The third panel, the backward pass computing gradients with respect to the weights themselves so the optimiser knows what to change, costs another two. A stacked bar at the bottom shows the forward pass is one third of the total cost and the backward pass is two thirds, which is the standard rule that backward costs about twice forward.">
  <rect x="14" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="132" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-accent">FORWARD</text>
  <text x="132" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="132" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">every weight is used once in</text>
  <text x="132" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">a multiply-accumulate:</text>
  <text x="132" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">one × and one +</text>

  <rect x="264" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="382" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-warm">BACKWARD — INPUT</text>
  <text x="382" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="382" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">the error has to keep travelling</text>
  <text x="382" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">to earlier layers:</text>
  <text x="382" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">∂L/∂x</text>

  <rect x="514" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="632" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-warm">BACKWARD — WEIGHTS</text>
  <text x="632" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="632" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">the optimiser needs to know</text>
  <text x="632" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">what to change:</text>
  <text x="632" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">∂L/∂W</text>

  <text x="60" y="204" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">SHARE OF THE TOTAL</text>
  <rect x="60"  y="214" width="220" height="34" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="170" y="236" class="t-xs t-mid t-b">forward — 2ND</text>
  <rect x="284" y="214" width="436" height="34" rx="5" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="502" y="236" class="t-xs t-mid t-b">backward — 4ND</text>

  <text x="60" y="278" class="t-xs t-muted">This is why "the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass" is a rule of thumb</text>
  <text x="60" y="294" class="t-xs t-muted">rather than a measurement: it is what the chain rule requires, not what a profiler found.</text>
</svg>
```
::: {.fig-cap}
Two for the forward pass, four for the backward pass, once per parameter per
token. Multiply by $N$ parameters and $D$ tokens and you have the run.
:::
::::

The forward two is the easy one. Every weight in a matrix multiply gets used
exactly once per token: one multiplication and one addition into the
accumulator. Two operations, per weight, per token.

The backward four is where people lose the thread, so name the two jobs
separately. Backpropagation through a layer must produce *two* different
gradients. It needs $\partial L/\partial x$ — how the loss changes with the
layer's *input* — or the error cannot propagate to the layer below. And it
needs $\partial L/\partial W$ — how the loss changes with each *weight* — or
the optimiser has nothing to update. Each of those is another matrix multiply
of the same shape, so each costs another 2 per parameter per token. Two jobs,
two each, four total.

### Does it agree with what the labs publish?

| run | $N$ | $D$ | $6ND$ | published | difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GPT-3 | 175B | 300B | $3.150\times10^{23}$ | $3.14\times10^{23}$ | +0.32% |
| Llama 3 405B | 405B | 15.6T | $3.791\times10^{25}$ | $3.80\times10^{25}$ | −0.24% |

Under half a percent, across a factor of 120 in compute and four years of
architecture change. It is tempting to call this a validation of the law. It is
not, and the distinction matters more than the agreement does.

[Those published figures are themselves $6ND$.]{.hl} GPT-3's Appendix D prints
the arithmetic in columns — "Fwd-pass flops per active param per token: 2",
"Mult for bwd pass: 3", "Flops per param per token: 6" — and states the
assumption openly: "we ignore the attention operation, as it typically uses
less than 10% of the total compute for the models we are analyzing"
[@brown2020language]. Llama 3's $3.8\times10^{25}$ is likewise a *budget*: the
number Meta fixed in advance and then chose a model size to fit
[@grattafiori2024llama3].

So the table shows that our bookkeeping matches theirs, which is worth
confirming and is all it is. The reason to trust $6ND$ is the derivation in the
figure above, not this table. What the table does buy you is practical: since
the labs count this way, you can read any announcement that gives parameters
and tokens and reconstruct the number they would quote — and, as the next
section shows, know exactly what that number leaves out.

### Where it stops being true

$6ND$ counts the matrix multiplies whose cost is proportional to parameters.
Attention's score matrix is not one of those: it depends on the *sequence
length*, which appears nowhere in $N$ or $D$.

@sec-attention-cost gives attention's forward cost for a whole sequence as
$4n^2d$ per layer. Three steps turn that into a per-token figure: divide by $n$
to get $4nd$ per token, halve it because causal masking means the average
position attends to only half the sequence, then multiply by 3 because the
backward pass costs twice the forward. That leaves about $6\,L\,n\,d$ per token
for $L$ layers, sequence length $n$, and width $d$.

How much does ignoring it matter? Exactly as much as your context is long.

| model and context | $6N$ per token | attention per token | attention as share of $6N$ | true cost ÷ $6ND$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3 8B at 8K context | $4.82\times10^{10}$ | $6.44\times10^{9}$ | 13% | 1.13× |
| Llama 3 8B at 128K context | $4.82\times10^{10}$ | $1.03\times10^{11}$ | 214% | 3.14× |
| Llama 3 405B at 8K context | $2.43\times10^{12}$ | $1.02\times10^{11}$ | 4% | 1.04× |

Read the last column as "what you should multiply $6ND$ by to get the truth".

::: {.column-margin}
There is a smaller error pushing the other way. The input embedding is a
*lookup*, not a matrix multiply, so it costs essentially no FLOPs — yet its
parameters are counted in $N$. Llama 3 8B's untied embedding is $128{,}256
\times 4096 = 525$M parameters, **6.5%** of its $N$; in the wider models the
embedding's share shrinks to only 1.5% of the 70B's and 0.5% of the 405B's. So $6ND$ over-counts small models slightly at
the same time as it under-counts attention. For the 8B at 8K the two partly
cancel.
:::

Two lessons, both practical. First, [$6ND$ is a *pretraining* law]{.hl}: it is
accurate because pretraining runs at short context, and the 405B is the most
accurate case of all because a wide model buries the attention term. Second,
at 128K context the true cost is more than three times what the law says —
which is precisely why long-context training is done as a short separate stage
on a fraction of the tokens rather than for the whole run.

### One run, end to end

Take Llama 3.1 405B and follow it from parameters to an invoice. Every input
is published: the paper gives $N$ and $D$, Meta's model card gives the
GPU-hours [@grattafiori2024llama3].

| quantity | value | where it comes from |
|:--|--:|:--|
| parameters | 405B | the paper |
| training tokens | 15.6T | the paper |
| compute | $3.79\times10^{25}$ FLOPs | $6ND$ |
| H100-hours | 30.84M | Meta's model card |
| on 8,000 H100s | 160.6 days | 30.84M ÷ 8,000 ÷ 24 |
| on 16,000 H100s | 80.3 days | the fleet actually used |
| on 24,000 H100s | 53.5 days | |
| rented at \$2.00/GPU-hour | ≈ \$62M | market rate, varies wildly |
| rented at \$3.00/GPU-hour | ≈ \$93M | |

Meta's card puts the whole Llama 3.1 family at **39.3M H100-hours**: 1.46M for
the 8B, 7.0M for the 70B, and 30.84M for the 405B. The 405B alone is 78% of
the family's compute.

::: {.column-margin}
Nobody rents 16,000 H100s by the hour, so the dollar figures are an
*opportunity cost*, not a bill Meta paid. They are still the right number for
you, because renting is exactly how you would reproduce any of this.
:::

### The brochure and the datacentre

Now the number that separates people who have run a cluster from people who
have read about one.

An H100 SXM is rated at **989 TFLOP/s** for dense BF16. (You will also see
1,979, which is the same chip with 2:4 structured sparsity — a different
operation that pretraining does not use. The PCIe card is about a quarter
slower again, at 756 TFLOP/s dense.
Check which number you are being quoted before comparing anything.) Divide the
FLOPs a run needed by the FLOPs its GPUs could have
produced in the hours it was allocated, and you get [model FLOPs
utilization](#gloss-model-flops-utilization){#term-model-flops-utilization .term-ref}: the fraction of the theoretical peak that actually became
training.

::: {#gloss-model-flops-utilization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**model FLOPs utilization** — the share of a chip's rated peak throughput that a real training run achieves, usually written *MFU*. Above 50% is rare; the gap is communication, memory bandwidth, and downtime. [↩](#term-model-flops-utilization){.term-back}
:::

The Llama 3 paper reports instantaneous BF16 MFU of **43%** on 8,000 GPUs,
**41%** on 16,000, and **38%** during the 128K-context stage
[@grattafiori2024llama3]. Here is what falls out of the published GPU-hours:

| model | GPU-hours | $6ND$ | effective MFU |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1.46M | $7.23\times10^{23}$ | 13.9% |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 7.00M | $6.35\times10^{24}$ | 25.5% |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 30.84M | $3.79\times10^{25}$ | 34.5% |

::: {.column-margin}
The 8B and 70B token counts come from the card's prose, "~15 trillion
tokens" — its spec table says "15T+" for the same runs. Only the 405B's 15.6T
is stated precisely, and only in the paper. A few percent of slack in $D$ does not
change the picture.
:::

Look at the 405B row against the paper's own 41%. The run delivered 34.5%.
Where did the missing 6.5 points go? Two places, and it is worth separating
them, because one is a fact about datacentres and the other is a fact about
our own arithmetic.

**Most of it is probably downtime.** The paper says so in a sentence that is
easy to skim past. During a 54-day snapshot of pretraining there were **466 job
interruptions** — 47 planned, 419 unexpected — and the run sustained ">90%
effective training time" [@grattafiori2024llama3]. Take that bound as exactly
0.90 and apply one stage's 41% to the whole run, and:

$$
41\% \times 0.90 = 36.9\%
$$

Both of those are choices, so 36.9% is an illustrative figure rather than a
number the paper reports. On that reading it would account for **4.1** of the
6.5 points. Not bad kernels, not a weak
framework, not incompetence. Hardware fails, a node drops out, the job
restarts from the last checkpoint and redoes work. At 16,000 GPUs running for
weeks, something breaking every three hours is not a crisis — it is the
weather.

**The rest looks like our own accounting, not the cluster's.** We estimated the
numerator as $6ND$, and $6ND$ omits attention. Standard MFU accounting counts
the model's attention matrix multiplies as useful work (it leaves out only
extra work such as recomputing activations to save memory), and the paper's
MFU presumably follows that convention; our numerator does not include
attention at all. We
are comparing two different measurements and calling the difference waste.
Add attention back, using the $6Lnd$-per-token correction we derived above and
the paper's own schedule — 8K context for the bulk of the run, then
"approximately 800B training tokens" ramping through six stages to 128K
[@grattafiori2024llama3]:

| model | $6ND$ only | attention-corrected | 41% $\times\,0.90$, illustrative |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 13.9% | 15.8–17.2% | not published |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 25.5% | 27.4–29.0% | not published |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 34.5% | **36.0–37.1%** | **36.9%** |

The ranges bracket the long-context tail: the low end assumes it all ran at
8K, the high end at the full 128K, and the truth is somewhere between because
the context grew in stages. Only the 405B has a published MFU to check
against — the paper's Table 4 covers "each stage of Llama 3 405B
pre-training" and says nothing about the smaller runs. [For that one model the
corrected range brackets the figure predicted from the paper's own
numbers]{.hl}: 36.0–37.1% around a predicted 36.9%, which is as close as this
kind of reconstruction gets. The brochure, the paper, and the
invoice agree once you stop comparing apples to oranges.

::: {.column-margin}
The same Table 4 reports **430 TFLOP/s per GPU** at the 43% stage. $430/989 =
43.5\%$ — which confirms the paper is quoting against the *dense* 989 peak,
not the sparsity number. Always worth checking.
:::

Two lessons, and the second is the one that will save you: interruptions are a
real and large tax that no amount of kernel tuning removes, and **an MFU
number means nothing until you know what went in the numerator.** When a
vendor quotes you utilization, ask.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Why the 8B still looks so much worse.** The attention correction lifts the
8B only to 15.8–17.2%, still less than half the 405B's. That is not the same
phenomenon and should not be explained the same way. Small models are harder
to keep an accelerator busy with: less arithmetic per unit of communication,
less work to hide latency behind, and a parallelism layout tuned for a 405B
sibling sharing the same cluster. The published GPU-hours are also *allocated*
hours, which include evaluation, checkpointing, and idle time that the paper's
instantaneous figure excludes — and with no published MFU for the 8B run there
is nothing to check the reconstruction against. Treat the 8B row as an upper
bound on waste, not a measurement of kernel quality — and treat the general
pattern as reliable: [big runs are efficient per GPU, small runs are
not]{.hl}.
:::

### Estimate your own run

Everything above is four multiplications. Change the inputs and watch which
one dominates.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preN = Inputs.range([0.1, 500], { value: 8, step: 0.1, label: "Parameters (billions)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preD = Inputs.range([1, 20000], { value: 300, step: 1, label: "Training tokens (billions)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preMfu = Inputs.range([5, 60], { value: 35, step: 0.5, label: "Effective MFU (%)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preGpu = Inputs.select(
  ["H100 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s", "A100 BF16 — 312 TFLOP/s", "H200 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s"],
  { value: "H100 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s", label: "Accelerator" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preFleet = Inputs.range([8, 32000], { value: 512, step: 8, label: "GPUs in the fleet" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof prePrice = Inputs.range([0.5, 8], { value: 2.5, step: 0.1, label: "Rental price per GPU-hour (USD)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
preCalc = {
  const peak = preGpu.startsWith("A100") ? 312e12 : 989e12;
  const N = preN * 1e9;
  const D = preD * 1e9;
  const flops = 6 * N * D;
  const gpuSeconds = flops / (peak * (preMfu / 100));
  const gpuHours = gpuSeconds / 3600;
  const days = gpuHours / preFleet / 24;
  const dollars = gpuHours * prePrice;
  const perParam = D / N;
  return { flops, gpuHours, days, dollars, perParam, peak };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:0.95rem">
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">compute</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${preCalc.flops.toExponential(2)} FLOPs</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">GPU-hours</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.gpuHours >= 1e6
          ? (preCalc.gpuHours / 1e6).toFixed(2) + "M"
          : Math.round(preCalc.gpuHours).toLocaleString("en-US")
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">wall clock on ${preFleet.toLocaleString("en-US")} GPUs</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.days < 1
          ? (preCalc.days * 24).toFixed(1) + " hours"
          : preCalc.days.toFixed(1) + " days"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">rental cost</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.dollars >= 1e6
          ? "$" + (preCalc.dollars / 1e6).toFixed(1) + "M"
          : "$" + Math.round(preCalc.dollars).toLocaleString("en-US")
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">tokens per parameter</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${preCalc.perParam.toFixed(1)}${
        preCalc.perParam < 20 ? " — under Chinchilla" : ""
      }</td></tr>
</table>`
```

Three settings worth typing in.

**8B parameters, 15,000B tokens, 14% MFU** reproduces Llama 3.1 8B. The table
reads **1.44M GPU-hours** against the **1.46M** Meta published — the last 1.4%
is the slider's half-point step (13.9% would land on the nose) and the fact that
the real model has 8.03B parameters, not 8.00B. Close enough that you can
trust the tool.

**405B and 15,600B at 35%** reproduces the flagship: 30.42M GPU-hours against
a published 30.84M. Nudge the MFU slider down one step to **34.5%** — the
effective figure we computed two sections ago — and it reads 30.86M, which is
the published number. That is the whole trick: [once you know a run's real
MFU, four multiplications reproduce its invoice]{.hl}.

**10B and 200B at 35%** is a serious academic run — 20.0 tokens per parameter,
exactly Chinchilla-optimal, for about **9,600 GPU-hours** and **\$24,000** at
\$2.50/hour. Now drop the fleet from 512 to **64**, which is closer to what a
well-funded university lab actually owns, and watch the wall clock go from
under a day to **6.3 days**. Then raise the tokens until it stops being
acceptable. That last step is the real lesson: [the binding constraint is
almost never the FLOPs, it is the calendar]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The H200 option is deliberately a no-op.** Look at the code: it computes the
same 989 TFLOP/s as the H100, so picking it changes nothing. That is not a
bug. Per NVIDIA's own datasheets the two chips have identical BF16 tensor-core
throughput; what differs is memory — **80 GB at 3.35 TB/s** on the H100 versus
**141 GB of HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s** on the H200. An H200 buys you bigger batches
and longer contexts without sharding as hard, which shows up as a *better
achievable MFU*, not as more peak FLOP/s. So if you want to model one, leave
the accelerator alone and raise the MFU slider instead.

[Memory capacity and memory bandwidth are what you are usually short of, not
arithmetic]{.hl} — and that is a lesson this calculator structurally cannot
teach you, because $6ND$ does not know memory exists. Keep it in mind every
time a formula in this chapter gives you a clean answer.
:::

### Who actually followed Chinchilla?

@sec-scaling-laws gave the compute-optimal ratio: about 20 tokens per
parameter [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]. Nobody shipping a model obeys it.

| model | tokens per parameter |
|:--|--:|
| GPT-3 175B | 1.7 |
| Chinchilla 70B | 20.0 |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 38.5 |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 212.5 |
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1,868.0 |

GPT-3 sits an order of magnitude *below* the line, which is exactly the
finding Chinchilla was published to correct — it was badly undertrained. Every
Llama sits above it, and the small models sit absurdly above it: the 8B saw
almost **1,900 tokens per parameter**, ninety-three times what compute-optimal
training would recommend.

This is not a mistake and it is not fashion. It is a different optimisation
with a different objective.

### Train once, serve forever

Chinchilla minimises the cost of *reaching* a given loss. If you are going to
serve the model, that is the wrong objective, because training is paid once
and inference is paid on every request until the model is retired.

The arithmetic is short. Generating one token costs about $2N$ FLOPs — the
forward pass only, no backward. So for Llama 3.1 8B:

$$
\underbrace{7.23\times10^{23}}_{\text{training}} \;\Big/\;
\underbrace{1.61\times10^{10}}_{\text{per generated token}} \;=\; 4.5\times10^{13}
$$

[Forty-five trillion generated tokens, and the serving FLOPs have equalled the
training FLOPs.]{.hl} A service producing 100 billion tokens a day passes that
point in 450 days. Any product with real usage crosses it.

Say what that point is and is not. It is FLOP parity for *one* model: the moment
its lifetime inference has cost as much arithmetic as its training. It is not
the point at which extra pretraining pays for itself, because training the same
model on more tokens does not lower its inference cost per token — the parameter
count does that. The break-even that answers "should we have trained longer" is
between two models of *equal quality*: $A$, the smaller one trained longer, and
$B$, the larger one trained to the compute-optimal point. It is
$T_{\text{break}} = (\text{Train}_A - \text{Train}_B)/(\text{Serve}_B - \text{Serve}_A)$
generated tokens, where Serve is the cost per token, which is the calculation that makes a smaller, longer-trained model
worth its extra training run. And the build-versus-buy question is a third
thing again, comparing training plus deployment plus operations against an API
invoice.

**And 45 trillion is the most favourable number you will ever get.** It
compares FLOPs to FLOPs, which quietly assumes a generated token and a trained
token cost the same to produce. They do not, for two reasons that both push
the same way:

- *Decode is memory-bound, not compute-bound.* Generating one token at a time
  means reading the entire weight matrix out of memory to do a single small
  matrix-vector product. Training reads those same weights once and amortises
  them over thousands of tokens in a batch. Where pretraining sustains 35–40%
  MFU, decode typically runs at a few percent — the chip is waiting on memory,
  not computing.
- *Prefill is free in this formula and is not free in life.* Every *input*
  token also costs $2N$, and most real workloads send far more input than they
  receive back. A long system prompt, a retrieved document, a chat history: all
  paid for, none of it counted above.

Redo the comparison in GPU-hours instead of FLOPs — the thing you actually
rent — against the 8B's published 1.46M H100-hours:

| decode efficiency | break-even | at 100B tokens/day |
|:--|--:|--:|
| 13.9% MFU | 45.0T tokens | 15 months |
| 10% MFU (large batches, well tuned) | 32.4T tokens | 11 months |
| 5% MFU | 16.2T tokens | 5 months |
| 2% MFU (typical interactive serving) | 6.5T tokens | **2 months** |

Look at the first row and at the 8B's effective MFU back in the table above.
They are the same 13.9%, and that is not a coincidence: [dividing FLOPs by
FLOPs silently assumes your decode server is exactly as efficient as Meta's
training cluster was]{.hl}. Written down like that, the assumption is obviously
untenable — the whole point of decode is that it cannot batch the way training
does.

So 45 trillion is an upper bound, and the real crossover is somewhere between
about two months and just over a year of serious traffic. Which only sharpens the argument:
overtraining pays back faster than the clean formula suggests, not slower.

That is the whole justification for training an 8B model on 15 trillion
tokens. You spend 93× the compute-optimal token budget for an 8B model up
front, to get a model that is permanently cheaper to run than the larger
compute-optimal model that would reach the same quality with less training
compute. The bigger, "correct" model would have been cheaper to train and more
expensive forever.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The same arithmetic makes the first cut on your build-versus-buy question.**
Work out the *total* tokens you expect the model to generate over its
lifetime, multiply by the model's $2N$, and compare to that model's training
compute. If you are three orders of magnitude below it, you are a rounding
error in someone else's inference fleet and you should be renting, not
training. Most teams are. The full comparison that actually decides it — API
bill against training plus deployment plus operations — is interview question
3 in @sec-pretraining-interview.
:::

## The model landscape {#sec-model-landscape}

Everything so far explains why there are perhaps a dozen organisations on
earth doing stage 1 at frontier scale, and why the rest of us are choosing
among their outputs. So: how do you tell those outputs apart?

Not by the word "open". [A release is not open or closed; it is a set of four
independent decisions]{.hl}, and vendors mix them freely.

The columns are independent. A release can publish weights and withhold data;
it can use a permissive licence on a model nobody can reproduce. "Open" alone
tells you nothing about which.
:::
::::

### What each column buys you

**Weights** buy you deployment. Given them — this is what makes something an
[open-weights model](#gloss-open-weights-model){#term-open-weights-model .term-ref} — you can run it on your own hardware, in
your own country, with no request leaving your network, which for a Turkish
institution subject to KVKK is frequently the entire argument. You can also
fine-tune, quantize, and inspect activations.

::: {#gloss-open-weights-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**open-weights model** — one whose trained parameters you can download and run yourself. It says nothing about whether the training data, the training code, or a permissive licence came with them; those are three separate questions. [↩](#term-open-weights-model){.term-back}
:::

**Training data** buys you audit. Without it you cannot check whether your
evaluation set leaked into training [@oren2024proving; @magar2022data] — the
problem called *benchmark contamination*: if the test items were in the
training data, a high score may measure memorisation rather than
capability. Without the data you also cannot
tell whether your language was represented, cannot answer a lawyer asking
where the text came from [@longpre2024audit], and cannot investigate a
memorised passage that turns up in production.

**Training code** buys you reproduction and, more usefully, *modification* —
being able to run the recipe on your own corpus rather than starting from a
paper.

**The licence** buys you the right to do all of the above in a product. This
is the column that most often surprises people, because "open weights" and
"open source" are routinely used as synonyms and are not.

It is also the column that varies *within* a row, which is why the diagram
says "varies" rather than picking a symbol. All three models named in the
middle row publish weights and withhold data and code — but Mistral 7B and
most Qwen 2.5 sizes are released under plain **Apache 2.0**, the same licence
the fully open models use, while Llama 3.1 carries **custom terms**. [Two
releases can be identical on three columns and differ completely on the
fourth]{.hl}, so there is no shortcut here: you have to check the specific
model. Sometimes you must check the specific *size*: Qwen 2.5's 3B and 72B
models ship under Qwen's own licences rather than Apache 2.0.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Read the licence before the benchmark table.** The Llama 3.1 Community
Licence is permissive for nearly everyone and is not an open-source licence.
Three concrete conditions, from the licence text itself:

- if your product had **more than 700 million monthly active users** in the
  month before the release date, you must request a separate licence from
  Meta, which Meta "may grant … in its sole discretion";
- you must display **"Built with Llama"** and ship a copy of the agreement;
- any model you train or improve using Llama or its outputs, and then
  distribute or make available, must have a name that **begins with
  "Llama"**.

None of those will stop a university project or most companies. All of them
are conditions that an OSI-approved licence such as Apache 2.0 does not
impose, which is exactly why the distinction has a name. OLMo, by contrast,
releases code and weights under Apache 2.0 and its pretraining corpus Dolma
under the ODC-BY data licence [@groeneveld2024olmo; @soldaini2024dolma] — and
its successors have kept that commitment.
:::

**The names in the grid go out of date quickly; the grid does not.** The
examples above are 2024 releases. Since then the open-weights row has filled
with large mixture-of-experts models under different licences — DeepSeek-R1
under MIT, Qwen3 under Apache 2.0, Llama 4 under another custom community
licence — and OpenAI, the best-known API-only lab, released open-weights
models of its own (gpt-oss, August 2025, Apache 2.0). So a row describes a
*release*, not a company: one lab can sit in two rows at once. Check each
release on all four columns, on the day you choose it.

The fully-open row exists for a reason that matters more to a university than
to a startup: [it is the row on which controlled replication and ablation are
straightforward.]{.hl} If you want to
ask "does adding Turkish data at 5% help or hurt English?", you need the data
and the code, not just the weights. The Pile [@gao2020pile], RefinedWeb
[@penedo2023refinedweb], Dolma [@soldaini2024dolma], and FineWeb
[@penedo2024fineweb] exist so that question can be asked at all.

### Reading a model card critically {#sec-model-cards}

A [model card](#gloss-model-card){#term-model-card .term-ref} is a short structured document describing what a model is, what
it was trained on, and where it should not be used [@mitchell2019model]; the
same idea applied to datasets is a datasheet [@gebru2021datasheets]. They are
now standard, which means they are now marketing as well as documentation.
Read them the way you would read a drug label: the useful information is
specific, and the interesting information is what has been left out.

::: {#gloss-model-card .column-margin .term-gloss}
**model card** — the document a lab publishes alongside a model, stating its intended use, training data, evaluation results, and limitations. Voluntary, unaudited, and still the most useful page you will read about a model. [↩](#term-model-card){.term-back}
:::

Work through Llama 3.1's card, which is better than most, and the technique
becomes clear.

| what the card says | how to read it |
|:--|:--|
| "15T+ tokens" in the table, "~15 trillion" in the prose | a floor and an approximation, on one page. The paper's 15.6T is the real one |
| "cutoff of December 2023" | hard, checkable, and the single most useful line on the card |
| supported languages: English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, Thai | **Turkish is not on the list** |
| "trained on a broader collection of languages than the 8 supported" | so the list is a *support* boundary, not a capability measurement |
| "11,390 tons CO2eq" location-based, "0 tons" market-based | the same training compute (all three models combined), two accounting standards, both true |
| benchmark tables | the model was tuned while these were visible; treat as an upper bound |

The language row is the one to think hardest about. The card puts use "in
languages beyond those explicitly referenced" **out of scope** — and yet our
own measurement two sections ago found Llama 3's tokenizer handling Turkish at
1.23× English, tied with multilingual BERT for the best of the multilingual
tokenizers tested. Both
statements are accurate. The card is telling you what Meta will stand behind,
not what the model can do.

[That gap is the whole reason you measure.]{.hl} A card cannot tell you
whether a model is good at *your* task in *your* language, because the vendor
did not evaluate that. For Turkish, nobody is going to do this for you.

Four questions no card answers, which you should therefore ask yourself:

1. **Was my evaluation set in the training data?** You usually cannot know.
   Assume contamination on any public benchmark older than the model, and keep
   a private held-out set [@kapoor2023leakage; @oren2024proving].
2. **How much of my language was in there?** Llama 3's 8% multilingual slice
   is shared across dozens of languages. Assume small.
3. **What does the model do at the boundary of its documented scope?** Test
   it. That is what @sec-llm-eval is for.
4. **What happens when this model is deprecated?** For an API, the answer may
   be "your prompts stop working on a schedule you do not control". For open
   weights, the answer is "nothing", and that is a real feature with a real
   price.

### Choosing one, in practice

The decision has four inputs and they are usually considered in the wrong
order. Capability first is the wrong order, because capability is the
constraint you are least likely to bind on and the most expensive to
over-buy.

Ask them like this instead:

1. **Where is the data allowed to be?** If personal data cannot leave the
   country or the building, the API row is gone and no benchmark score brings
   it back. Decide this first; it eliminates more options than anything else.
2. **What does the licence permit?** Check the user-count clause, the naming
   clause, and the attribution clause against your actual product. Do this
   second, while it is still cheap to change your mind.
3. **What can you afford to serve?** From the arithmetic above: $2N$ FLOPs per
   generated token. Multiply by your expected traffic. This usually chooses
   your parameter count for you, and it usually chooses something smaller than
   you assumed.
4. **Only now, is it good enough?** Evaluate the survivors on *your* data.
   The public leaderboard is a screening tool at best, and after contamination
   it is barely that.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The default that is right more often than it should be.** Start with the
smallest open-weights model that clears your quality bar on your own
evaluation set, and treat a frontier API as the thing you escalate to for the
hard tail of requests. It is cheaper, it is private, it does not change under
you, and — from the break-even arithmetic above — the economics improve every
month your traffic grows. @sec-serving takes this apart properly.
:::

## Lab: price a Turkish pretraining run {#sec-pretraining-lab}

Everything in this lab is arithmetic and tokenizer calls. Nothing here needs a
GPU — which is the point, because the decision this chapter is about gets made
long before anyone touches a GPU.

1. **Measure fertility on your own text.** Take 2,000–5,000 sentences of
   Turkish from a domain you care about — support tickets, legal text, news,
   clinical notes, your own thesis. Tokenize with at least four tokenizers:
   one English-first (`openai-community/gpt2`), two multilingual
   (`NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B`, `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B`), and one Turkish-native
   (`dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased`). Those are the exact identifiers behind
   the table in @sec-tokenizer-budget, so your numbers should reproduce ours
   on the same corpus. Report tokens-per-word and total tokens for each. Do
   **not** report tokens-per-word alone as a cross-language claim; you now
   know why.
2. **Get the honest ratio.** Translate — or find an existing parallel
   version of — 200 of those sentences into English. Recompute the ratio on
   matched content. State how far your domain's number is from this chapter's
   1.23× for Llama 3, and give one concrete reason for the gap. Domain
   vocabulary is the usual culprit: proper nouns, code, numbers and acronyms
   tokenize almost identically in both languages and drag the ratio toward 1.
3. **Turn the ratio into money.** Pick a real API price list. Compute what
   one million of your Turkish documents costs to process under each
   tokenizer's ratio. Then compute the same figure for the English
   translations. The difference is the surcharge, in your currency, for your
   product.
4. **Find the context ceiling.** For a 128K-token context window, compute how
   many Turkish *words* fit under each tokenizer, and how many English words
   fit. Report both. This is the number that decides whether a document fits
   in the context window in one piece or has to be split and served piece by
   piece through retrieval (@sec-retrieval).
5. **Budget a run with $C = 6ND$.** Suppose you want a Turkish-first base
   model. Choose $N$ and $D$ yourself and justify both: $N$ from what you
   intend to serve (@sec-serving), $D$ from what Turkish text actually exists
   at the quality you need. Use the calculator in @sec-pretraining-compute to
   get FLOPs, GPU-hours, wall-clock on a fleet you could plausibly rent, and a
   dollar figure. Then state your assumed MFU and defend it — if you wrote
   down a number above 40%, say which paper you are matching.
6. **Sanity-check against reality.** Compare your budget to the three
   published Llama 3.1 runs. If your number is far smaller, find the
   assumption doing the work. It is almost always MFU or the token count.
7. **Now do the sensitivity analysis.** Recompute the run's cost with 1.23×
   more tokens — the Turkish surcharge applied to the *training* corpus, not
   just inference. Report the extra dollars. Then answer the question the
   number poses: at what point does it become cheaper to train a Turkish
   tokenizer and a smaller model than to pay the surcharge on a multilingual
   one forever?
8. **Compute your own break-even, twice.** Using $2N$ FLOPs per generated
   token, find how many tokens your service must generate before serving
   costs exceed training. That is the FLOP-parity answer, and you now know it
   is an upper bound. So do it again in GPU-hours, assuming decode sustains
   2–5% MFU against your training run's 35%. Convert both to months at your
   projected traffic. If the honest answer is under a year, you have just
   discovered why inference-optimal and compute-optimal are different
   objectives.

**Deliverable:** a one-page memo — the kind you would actually send — that
recommends *train*, *fine-tune*, or *use an API* for a specific Turkish
product, with the same-content ratio table, the compute budget, and the break-even
month as its three pieces of evidence. State the assumption that, if wrong,
would flip your recommendation.

## Intuition checks {#sec-pretraining-intuition}

Answer before expanding. Each is a place where the intuitive answer is wrong in
a direction that costs money — which is the recurring theme of pretraining
decisions you inherit and cannot undo.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. With Llama 3's tokenizer, Turkish needs 2.12 tokens per word and English needs 1.28. Does Turkish cost 66% more?

No. It costs about 23% more, and the comparison is invalid as posed.

Tokens-per-word compares units of different size. Turkish is agglutinative:
*evlerinizden* is one word meaning "from your houses". [The honest measurement
is tokens for the *same content*]{.hl} — tokenize a sentence and its
professional translation and divide.

Do that on 1,157 aligned pairs and BERTurk costs **0.58×** what English costs;
the Turkish-native tokenizers are the only ones where Turkish is *cheaper*.
GPT-2 costs **1.98×**, Llama 3 and multilingual BERT **1.23×**.

The same corpus is 8,058 Turkish words against 10,862 English words of matched
content — the agglutination is visible in the raw counts before any tokenizer
touches it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your model tokenizes Turkish badly. Can you fine-tune your way out of it?

Not with an ordinary fine-tune, and that is why the tokenizer belongs in a
pretraining chapter rather than a preprocessing one.

Changing the tokenizer changes the embedding table, which changes every weight
downstream. It is not impossible: you can extend the vocabulary, initialise the
new embeddings from the pieces they replace, and continue pretraining until the
model settles — a documented and occasionally worthwhile procedure, and
vocabulary-adaptation methods exist that initialise the new rows from the old
ones rather than from scratch. What it is not is free or safe. Its cost scales
with how much of the vocabulary you change, what you start from and what quality
you will accept, and it risks degrading things the model already does well; it
is not automatically a second pretraining run, and it is not an ordinary
fine-tune either. [The tokenizer is how the compute budget gets divided between
languages, and undoing that division is a project with its own budget.]{.hl}
Absent
that project, a user of a 1.98× tokenizer pays the surcharge in context window,
in latency, and on every API invoice, for the life of the model.

Llama 3 shows the decision being made deliberately: 100,000 tokens from
`tiktoken` plus **28,000 added specifically for non-English languages**,
reported as improving compression for those languages with no cost to English.
That is a design choice with a price tag, made once, before the first gradient
step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A vendor quotes 40% MFU. Is that good?

Unanswerable until you ask what went in the denominator, and asking is the
whole point of the question.

The same GPU has a dense peak and a sparsity peak twice as large, and the
denominator decides the answer: dividing by the larger one *halves* the
reported MFU. Llama 3's Table 4 reports 430 TFLOP/s per GPU; against the H100's
dense BF16 peak that is $430/989 = 43.5\%$, and against the 2:4-sparsity peak
the same run would report $430/1{,}979 = 21.7\%$. The 43.5% confirms they used the
dense figure. Two MFUs are comparable only when they used the same peak, and
nobody is obliged to tell you which they used.

The second trap is the numerator. Reconstructing Llama 3.1 405B from $6ND$
alone gives 34.5%; adding the attention term gives **36.0–37.1%**, which brackets the **36.9%** our illustrative 41% × 0.90 estimate predicts. [$6ND$ omits attention, which is fine for a
budget estimate and not fine for a utilization comparison.]{.hl}

Two numbers that look comparable and are not is the most common way engineering
conversations about efficiency go wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Where does the 6 in $C = 6ND$ come from?

Three twos, each with a cause, and knowing them is what lets you adapt the
formula instead of reciting it.

Two FLOPs per parameter in the **forward** pass, because each weight
participates in one multiply and one add. Two more for the **backward pass
through the inputs**, because the error has to keep travelling to earlier
layers. Two more for the **backward pass through the weights**, because the
optimiser needs to know what to change.

So the forward pass is $2ND$ and is only a third of the bill — which
immediately tells you that inference costs roughly $2N$ FLOPs *per token*
(hence $2ND$ for $D$ tokens), not $6N$, and that is the number that decides whether serving or training dominates your
budget. It also tells you why $6ND$ is a *pretraining* law and does not
transfer unchanged to fine-tuning with frozen weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. You have more compute. Should you train a bigger model or use more data?

Both, in roughly equal measure — and the interesting part is that this was the
field's mistake for two years.

Chinchilla's finding is that parameters and tokens should scale together;
earlier models were badly undertrained for their size. But the compute-optimal
answer is not the answer you want if you are going to *serve* the model:
[a smaller model trained longer costs more to train and less to run
forever]{.hl}, which is why production models are routinely trained well past
the compute-optimal point.

The lab's break-even question is the practical form: if your model serves for
more than a few months, inference-optimal and compute-optimal are different
objectives and the one you should be optimising is inference-optimal, not
compute-optimal.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Can you just train on the same data twice instead of collecting more?

Up to a point that is measurable and then not.

Muennighoff et al. found repeated data "yields negligible changes to loss
compared to having unique data" for up to about four epochs. Past that, each
further epoch is worth less; the paper still finds meaningful gains up to
around 16 epochs, after which returns fall off very fast and you are mostly
spending compute to memorise.

The practical reading for a language like Turkish: [the constraint on a
Turkish pretraining run is the corpus, not the GPUs]{.hl}, and repetition buys
you a small multiple rather than an escape. That is also why the data-filtering
decisions in @sec-pretraining-data get so much attention — when you cannot get
more text, what you keep matters much more.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-pretraining-interview}

Pretraining questions are rarely about whether you would run one. They are
about whether you can reason quantitatively about a system you inherited, which
is the actual job.

::: {.column-margin}
Almost nobody being interviewed has pretrained a model, and the interviewer
knows it. What separates answers is whether you can do the arithmetic that
decides *build, fine-tune, or buy* — and whether you know which pretraining
decisions you are stuck with afterwards.
:::

1. **Estimate the compute for a 7B model on 2 trillion tokens.** $C \approx 6ND
   = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} \approx 8.4\times10^{22}$
   FLOPs. Then convert to something a budget-holder understands: divide by the
   per-GPU throughput you actually expect — not peak, roughly 40% of dense peak
   — times 3,600 seconds, and you have GPU-hours. Say out loud that $6ND$
   ignores attention, which for a 7B model adds roughly 4% at 2K context, 8% at
   4K and 15% at 8K, and much more at long context, and that [the thing that actually blows up a pretraining schedule is
   almost never the FLOPs, it is the calendar]{.hl}: interruptions, restarts and
   checkpoint reloads.

2. **What is the single pretraining decision you cannot undo later?** The
   tokenizer. Everything else — instruction behaviour, safety, domain
   knowledge, even a good deal of factual content — can be moved by
   post-training (@sec-post-training). The tokenizer is the one that resists,
   because changing it means rebuilding the embedding table the rest of the
   weights were trained against — possible, but a project rather than a
   fine-tune. Quantify the
   stakes with the same-content ratio from the tokenizer table: a Turkish user on GPT-2's tokenizer pays
   **1.98×** the tokens of an English user for the same content, and on BERTurk
   **0.58×**. Same language, same text, a 3.4× spread driven entirely by a
   decision made before training started.

3. **How would you decide whether to pretrain, fine-tune, or use an API for a
   Turkish product?** Three numbers, in this order. The same-content ratio
   (Turkish ÷ English tokens), because it sets your per-content cost forever and may by itself justify a Turkish-native model.
   The $6ND$ budget for the smallest model that could work, which is almost
   always large enough to end the conversation. And the break-even month: the
   point where API spend at your projected traffic exceeds training plus
   serving. If that month is years away, buy. (This is the build-versus-buy
   break-even, not the inference-optimal one from @sec-pretraining-compute;
   keep the two apart.) The answer
   for nearly every product is *fine-tune or buy* — being able to show *why*
   with arithmetic is the skill.

4. **Where does pretraining data actually come from, and what is thrown away?**
   Common Crawl or a cleaned derivative such as FineWeb, and the honest headline
   is how much is discarded: filtering, deduplication and quality classification
   remove the large majority of raw crawl. Name the specific steps — boilerplate
   removal, language identification, deduplication across crawls, quality
   classifiers — and the counter-intuitive finding that FineWeb's authors hit:
   aggressive deduplication across *all* crawls made things worse, because it
   preferentially kept the low-quality text that had not been repeated.
   [Deduplication is not monotonically good]{.hl}, which is the kind of detail
   that shows you read the report rather than the summary.

5. **A model claims a 128K context window. What should you be sceptical about?**
   That the quality is uniform across it, and that you can afford it. On
   quality, training rarely happens at full length throughout — the context is
   usually extended in stages near the end — so the last 100K tokens have seen
   far less training than the first 8K. On cost, take @sec-attention-cost's
   arithmetic: with plain multi-head attention a 7B model's KV cache at 100,000 tokens is
   52.4 GB per concurrent request, against 14 GB of weights — but with the
   grouped-query attention that Llama 3 8B uses (8 KV heads instead of 32)
   the same cache is 13.1 GB. A 4× difference out of one line of config. The window being *advertised*
   and the window being *usable at your budget* are different numbers.

6. **Why do small pretraining runs look so much less efficient than large
   ones?** Because efficiency here is mostly about keeping an accelerator busy,
   and small models give it less to work with: less arithmetic per unit of
   communication, less work to hide latency behind. Reconstructed MFU for
   Llama 3.1 goes 15.8–17.2% at 8B, 27.4–29.0% at 70B, 36.0–37.1% at 405B. Then
   add the caveat that makes the answer honest: published GPU-hours are
   *allocated* hours including evaluation, checkpointing and idle time, and only
   the 405B has a published MFU to check against — so treat the 8B figure as an
   upper bound on waste rather than a measurement of kernel quality.

7. **Your Turkish (or Arabic, or Finnish) product costs far more per request than the English one. Explain and fix.**
   First compare how many tokens the same content produces under the tokenizer in
   use. Differences between languages can be related to the distribution of the
   training data, the vocabulary, the writing system and the tokenization rules
   [@petrov2023language]. In the cost of a request, also look separately at input
   and output lengths, model prices and any caching conditions. On the short
   parallel text in this chapter the Turkish/English token ratio was 1.82 for
   `cl100k_base` and 1.39 for `o200k_base`. Those figures illustrate a
   tokenizer-dependent difference; to estimate the cost ratio of your product,
   measure over a large number of representative requests. Fixes, in increasing
   order of effort: pick a model whose tokenizer produces fewer tokens in this
   language; measure cost in tokens per *task* rather than per request; given
   enough scale and training budget, consider training a domain- and
   language-specific tokenizer together with a compatible model, or adapting the
   existing model to it [@kudo2018sentencepiece]. The tokenizer of a pretrained
   model cannot be swapped like an independent part without making the model
   compatible.

8. **Explain BPE. What happens to a word the tokenizer has never seen?**
   Describe the merge loop, then answer the real question: nothing special happens.
   The word decomposes into known subwords, in the worst case single characters. If
   the base alphabet covers the input, or the tokenizer can write an unknown
   character as its bytes (byte fallback), there is no need for `<UNK>` because of
   an unrepresentable character. That coverage does not mean no information is
   removed during preprocessing, though; losslessness has to be assessed for the
   tokenization pipeline as a whole. For unknown characters the base alphabet and
   byte-fallback support are decisive; the algorithm's segmentation rules and the
   limits of the implementation matter too. The classic BERT WordPiece tokenizer
   can emit `[UNK]` for a character outside its vocabulary. Even with known
   characters, the word-length limit can give the same result: the mBERT tokenizer
   splits a word of 100 letters `a` into 50 pieces and turns one of 101 letters
   into a single `[UNK]`. Byte-level or byte-fallback designs write the unknown
   character as its bytes. Use the worked example from this chapter: the word
   `lowest`, absent from the BPE tokenizer's training example, is split into
   `low + est` by the learned merges.

## Where to go deeper

Two things are worth doing before reading any of the papers. Open
[FineWeb's interactive report](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1)
and read the ablation plots — it is the rare case where a lab published the
failed variants alongside the shipped one. Then open the
[tokenizer playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/the-tokenizer-playground)
and paste in the longest Turkish word you know; the whole of
@sec-tokenizer-budget becomes obvious in about ten seconds.

Then watch someone do it: Karpathy's
[Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l8pRSuU81PU)
is four hours of actual pretraining, which makes every number in this chapter
concrete, and
[Stanford CS336](https://stanford-cs336.github.io/spring2025/) is a whole
course built around doing it yourself.

**Tokenization, hands on.**

- **[Hugging Face LLM Course, Chapter 6](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/1)**.
  Builds BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenizers and explains which models use
  which. [The BPE lesson](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5)
  is the direct sequel to our toy implementation.
- **[minbpe](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe)** and the accompanying
  [two-hour video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE), Andrej
  Karpathy [@karpathy2024minbpe]. A few hundred lines of clean Python that
  build a GPT-grade tokenizer from scratch. Watch the video, then read the code
  line by line; the two were designed together.
- **[The Tokenizer Playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/the-tokenizer-playground)**.
  Paste text, switch tokenizers, watch the splits. Try your own name, your
  company's part numbers, and a paragraph of Turkish.
- **[tiktoken](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken)**. The library used for
  the cost measurements in this chapter.

The papers below are the ones this chapter's numbers came from. Read them in
roughly this order:

| topic | source |
|:--|:--|
| a full pretraining run, documented | @grattafiori2024llama3 |
| what the data pipeline does, with ablations | @penedo2024fineweb; @penedo2023refinedweb |
| the corpora, published in the open | @gao2020pile; @soldaini2024dolma |
| an end-to-end open model — weights, data, and code | @groeneveld2024olmo |
| why duplicates hurt | @lee2022deduplicating; @carlini2021extracting |
| how many epochs you may run | @muennighoff2023scaling |
| the compute-optimal frontier | @kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla |
| subword tokenization, at the source | @sennrich2016neural; @kudo2018sentencepiece |
| what tokenizers cost speakers of other languages | @petrov2023language |
| where the data actually came from, and its licences | @longpre2024audit; @dodge2021documenting |
| cards and datasheets | @mitchell2019model; @gebru2021datasheets |
| training on model output | @shumailov2024curse |
| the argument that scale beats cleverness | @sutton2019bitter |

## Exercises

1. Take one open model card and one closed model card. List three claims each
   makes that you could verify yourself, and three you cannot. Then state
   which of the six unverifiable claims would most change your decision if it
   turned out to be false.
2. The FineWeb team tested global deduplication with a pointed experiment.
   Inside the single old 2013-48 snapshot they took the ~31B tokens global
   dedup had **kept** and the ~460B tokens it had **removed** (re-deduplicated
   on their own, giving 171B), trained a model on each, and found the model
   trained on the *removed* data was better. Explain the mechanism — note that
   the experiment compares two slices of one snapshot, not two corpora, which
   is what makes it a clean test. Then name one filter elsewhere in the funnel
   that could fail in exactly the same way, and say what you would measure to
   catch it.
3. Llama 3's final annealing stage covers 40M tokens: 0.00026% of the run. In
   a separate annealing experiment on a mix that upweighted high-quality code
   and maths, the paper reports a **24.0%** GSM8k improvement on the 8B model
   and essentially nothing on the 405B. The paper does not say whether 24.0%
   is relative or in percentage points; say how each reading would change how
   impressed you should be. Then give an explanation consistent with both
   results. Your explanation
   should predict something — say what.
4. A vendor advertises 1,979 TFLOP/s for their accelerator. You measure a
   sustained 310 TFLOP/s on your own training job. Work through the gap in
   three named steps, using this chapter's figures for each, and state what
   fraction of the shortfall you could plausibly recover with better
   engineering versus what is structural.
5. Compute $6ND$ for a 3B model on 2T tokens. Then compute how many H100-hours
   it needs at 40% MFU, and how long that takes on 64 GPUs. Now recompute at
   25% MFU — the figure you should assume for a first run on a cluster nobody
   has tuned. Report both wall-clock numbers and say which one belongs in a
   project plan.
6. Our corpus measurement found Qwen 2.5 (vocab 151,643) tokenizing Turkish
   at 1.40× English, while Llama 3 (vocab 128,000) managed 1.23×. Explain why
   the larger vocabulary lost. Then design the smallest experiment that would
   confirm your explanation, and say what result would refute it.
7. For `evlerinizden`, Llama 3 produces `ev|ler|iniz|den` — four tokens that
   are exactly the four morphemes — while Cosmos GPT-2 produces
   `ev|lerinizden`: two tokens, half the cost, and a second token that is not
   a linguistic unit at all. Argue for each as the better segmentation. Then
   state what you would measure to settle it, and be specific about the task,
   because the answer is not the same for every task.
8. GPT-3 used 1.7 tokens per parameter; Llama 3.1's 8B used 1,868. Both were
   rational decisions. Reconstruct the reasoning behind each, then find the
   traffic level at which GPT-3's ratio would have been the correct choice
   for Meta.
9. You are given a fixed budget of 10,000 H100-hours — a realistic Turkish
   university allocation. Using this chapter's arithmetic, work out the
   largest model you could pretrain from scratch on a Chinchilla-optimal token
   count. Then argue, with numbers, for spending the same allocation on
   continued pretraining of an existing open-weights model instead. State
   which you would actually do and why.
10. Common Crawl's WET extraction "retained too much boilerplate and menu
    text", so FineWeb re-extracted from WARC with trafilatura. Boilerplate is
    highly repetitive. Explain why deduplication does not simply remove it,
    and what that tells you about the order of operations in a data pipeline.
11. **Tokenizer economics.** Take a paragraph of your own technical writing
    in Turkish and its English translation. Using the Tokenizer Playground or
    `tiktoken`, count tokens under two different tokenizers. First compute the
    ratio of token counts for the same content in the two languages. Then
    estimate the annual cost at 100,000 requests per month, using the unit prices
    of the model you choose and stating their date. Report input and output
    tokens, the shared prompt and any cached input separately, and state
    explicitly the assumption that one paragraph represents all requests.
12. **Measure the Turkish token cost over many examples.** The
    measurement above used one short pair of texts, and the 1.82 and 1.39 ratios
    there are not general. Collect 50 to 100 sentence pairs from a parallel text
    you have — articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a piece of
    software's interface strings in two languages, your own bilingual reports.
    For each tokenizer make two separate measurements: the Turkish/English ratio
    of token counts for each aligned pair, and the number of tokens per 1,000
    Unicode code points in each language. The first shows the token difference
    for the same content, the second the token density relative to the length of
    the writing. Report the median and the interquartile range; for an estimate
    of total cost, also use the total token counts over all examples and the
    expected distribution of requests. Where in that distribution did the
    single-pair measurement fall?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Expected observations for exercises 11 and 12

Not solutions — but knowing what you are meant to see makes it easier to check
yourself.

11. The Turkish paragraph can produce more tokens under some tokenizers. Measure
    the direction and size of the difference, and report the result together with
    the text pair and tokenizer version you chose.
12. Report the token density of each language and the token ratios of the aligned
    pairs separately. The direction and spread of the difference depend on the
    examples and on the tokenizer. A single example is one observation inside the
    distribution, not a summary of it.
:::
